He does the thing men do when they have to ask a stranger for help and have decided to lead with the thing that does not, technically, ask for help.

The hood, after a few seconds, has a small steady plume of steam coming out of it.
The two of them, at the engine, do the thing two people do at an engine that has just failed.

The passenger door opens. A woman gets out. She is maybe a year or two younger than the man. She is wearing a tank top and shorts. She fans herself with what looks, from the counter, like a folded brochure. She walks around to the front of the car and stands beside the man.

The driver gets out. The driver is — from her angle, through the front window, with the lottery-decal-and-dead-cigarette-brand layers between her and the lot — a man in his late twenties or early thirties. He is in a t-shirt that is the color t-shirts become when they have been worn three days in a row. He goes to the front of the car. He pops the hood.

Sam, at the counter, looks up because the car comes in slowly and stops in the lot's far corner instead of pulling up to a pump, and because the car is, on its surface, not a car she has seen in this lot before. The car is small. The car is European. The car is — she registers, in the way she has been registering things this summer — red, in the way of a car that has been red for forty years and that has, in the past five years, started to fade in the small uneven patches a forty-year-old red paint job fades in when the car has lived its life mostly outdoors.
[shot:establish]The red car pulls into the lot at nine forty-seven.
She returns to the counter.
The permission is its own weather.
She has, in the past two months, been getting better at the small permission.

She does not, after, look at it for a long minute. She wipes the counter. She refills the coffee. She rings up an older man for two scratch-offs and a coffee and, when he has left, allows herself permission of remembering that her boyfriend, the boy who is not, this summer, the boy who can be in her actual physical company for more than the small portions his nervous system permits, is — by his text — alive and on a road and going home to his grandmother and that this, today, is what she has.
She puts the phone down.
love you. i'll text later.

She reads it.

A construction guy comes in at eight-fourteen for a breakfast burrito and a coffee. A woman Sam has not seen before comes in at eight twenty-six for a pack of Marlboro Lights. A high school kid Sam vaguely recognizes from school comes in at eight forty-four for a Red Bull and a bag of jerky. By nine the store has had eleven customers, which is the standard Thursday morning rate, and Sam has — between rings — done the work of restocking the front cooler from the walk-in, which is a job that is technically Jen's and that Sam has, over two summers, stopped pointing out to Jen because Jen has stopped pretending Sam doesn't do it.
[shot:establish]The morning starts the way Thursday mornings start.

She is on the eight-to-four. Jen is at the back office doing the deposit paperwork from yesterday. Skip Donnelly's replacement at the Gas & Go across the intersection has been a guy named Rory since June, and Rory is, by Sam's eight-AM count of the cars in the Gas & Go lot, doing his job the way Skip used to: not very. Rory has, in three months, not noticed that Sam can see his customers from the Kwik Stop window. Sam has, in three months, decided that the not-noticing is one more piece of the small inheritance the spring has left her.
She wipes the counter.
[shot:insert coffee]She refills the coffee.
She ties on her apron.

The microwave clock, set nine minutes fast on purpose because Jen the day manager says it helps the closers, reads eight-eleven. The actual clock by the office door reads eight oh-two. Sam has, over two summers, stopped doing the small math of converting between them. The microwave is the closer-clock. The wall clock is the open-clock. Both are right in the small ways the Kwik Stop has decided they are right, and both are wrong in the small ways it has decided they are wrong, and Sam, at seventeen, has the small equanimity of a counter girl who has stopped requiring a single canonical time.
[mood:day_bright]Sam clocks in at eight oh-two.
He sleeps when the street sounds outside blur to a nothing in his mind.
He does not tell Lucy.
Mark, in Room 7, before he sleeps, thinks about his father.

Mark and Lucy, in Room 7 of the Cypress, are asleep by seven PM, having eaten the small early dinner the gas-station-adjacent McDonald's had provided them for fourteen dollars, and having decided, between them, that the Atlanta bus at six AM is going to be the bus they take and that the trip is, from this Kwik Stop on, going to be a bus trip and not a car trip, and that the Peugeot — Mark's father's car, which Mark has been, in some specific sense, driving since 2014 — is no longer his.
The Peugeot is, by Bobby's evening estimate, going to sit in his lot for at least three weeks before it becomes parts.
Bianca, on the porch, is reading.
[shot:establish]Outside, the Texas dusk is doing its slow gold thing.
The fan, in her bedroom, clicks on the third rotation. She has, over the summer, stopped counting. The clicks are, by August, just clicks.
She closes her eyes.
[beat:still]She thinks: it exists. That is enough.

She thinks: the small fact of one twenty, in cash, in a duffel bag walking east on the Linden access road in the August heat at eleven-thirty AM, is a fact that exists in the world tonight whether or not anyone but me and Mark and Lucy and Jen and the brochure remembers it.
She thinks: tomorrow I am going to be at the Kwik Stop again, eight to four. Friday is payday. The wallet refills. The world goes on.

She thinks: I have, in the past forty-eight days, become a person who can hand a stranger one twenty and not need to have the gratitude back. That is a thing I had not, in May, known I was going to be able to do.

The small fact of having one twenty in her wallet that she had handed to two strangers and that is no longer hers is — for tonight, at the kitchen table at four forty-eight — the small private weight she is, for one evening, going to carry alone.

Go play. They're waiting.

[shot:closeup walt]Carl told Nate. Nate told me at dinner Monday. The Foxhole is a real venue, Jess. You guys are — you guys are coming up. Don't make a big deal. But also — kid. That's a thing. I want you to know I know.

Walt is in the kitchen when Jesse comes in. He is in his work shirt, having just come home. He is making a sandwich.

Nate's garage is bigger than Jesse's. Nate's parents had, in 2018, converted the rear half of their two-car garage into a small finished room with sound dampening on the walls and a separate window AC that does not, technically, count as part of the house's HVAC envelope. The conversion had been Nate's father's project. Nate's father — a man in his fifties named Walt who works in commercial insurance and who plays the bass himself in a wedding band that performs three times a year — had finished the conversion the summer Nate had turned fifteen, with the small clarity of a man who had decided that his son was going to have, in their house, the room he himself had not had at fifteen in the house in Houston his own father had, in 1972, refused to let him put a drum kit into.
[mood:dusk][shot:establish]He pulls into Nate's driveway at seven oh-two.

Jesse has not, for two weeks, been able to confirm what is in the unit. The blue annotation is the only blue annotation on his map. The Foxhole is across the parking lot. He has not, until this afternoon's flyer, registered that the geography of his map and the geography of his band were, this Saturday, going to converge.

He had, in late July, registered that the unit at the rear of the strip mall — the one whose front-facing storefront window has been papered over since the previous tenant, a payday-loan operation, had closed in March — had begun, in the past three weeks, to be visited at night by a small white panel van. The van arrives between one and three AM. The van stays between forty and ninety minutes. The van leaves. There is no signage on the unit. There is no permit displayed in the window. The papered-over window has, by Jesse's three observations, been re-papered over twice since the original papering — once in early July, once in early August — in a way that suggests the paper has been lifted from the inside and then replaced.
The blue is the unit at the back of the strip mall on Live Oak Street that contains The Foxhole.
He has, by Wednesday evening, fourteen black, four red, and one blue.

It is not, by Ben's count, a My Sharona morning. My Sharona mornings are Mondays. Sweet Child o' Mine is Tuesdays and Thursdays. Eye of the Tiger is Wednesdays. Africa — Ben has not, over three weeks, placed Africa on a regular day, but Africa shows up about twice a week and always, when it does, near the end of a session.
The song this morning is Sweet Child o' Mine.

[shot:closeup coach_k]The driver's-side door is open. Coach K is at the tailgate loading the equipment cart with the morning's cones and the rope ladder and the canvas bag of mouthguards he carries to every session even though most of the kids bring their own. The cab speakers are at their usual volume, which is the volume of a man who does not, anymore, hear above eight kilohertz on his left side and has compensated by raising the master.

[shot:insert truck]The truck is the white Ford F-250 with the camper shell and the ladder rack and the tape job on the driver's-side mirror Coach K has been meaning to replace since spring. The truck is parked at the head of the lot, in the spot that has been Coach K's for as long as Ben has been at this high school — the spot closest to the field gate, the spot the assistant principal has, every August for some years, considered painting RESERVED — KAZANTZAKIS and has, every August, decided that painting it would be an admission of something, and has not.
[mood:dawn_warm]The truck is in the lot when Ben pulls in at five fifty-three.
Water. Five minutes. Then weights.
Water. Five minutes. Then weights.
The chart goes up at noon.
He drives back to the school.
He starts the car.

He has, in the past two hours, eaten a sandwich, sat with the dog, watched five minutes of the noon news, and had a forty-second exchange with his father at the kitchen table that was, by Bill's standard, one of the longest forty-second exchanges Bill has had with him this summer.
[mood:day_bright][shot:closeup ben~]In the Civic he sits for a count with both hands on the wheel.
Ben goes out the door.
[shot:insert crossword]He looks down at the crossword.
[beat:still]But thanks anyway.
Yeah.
Ben. The advice is free. The thanks is unnecessary.
I don't know. For — for the advice.
Ben thinks.
For what.
Thanks.
Yeah.
Bill looks up.
Dad.
He turns.
[shot:closeup ben]At the door he pauses.
Ben goes to the door.
I'll text you.
Yeah.
I figured.
I'm going back. Chart goes up at noon.
He gets up.
He looks at the time.

He eats the sandwich. He drinks two glasses of water. He sits with Daisy on the couch for twenty minutes. He watches, with the sound off, the noon news, which has — at twelve oh-five — a story about the heat that has been in every noon broadcast for three weeks and that says, today, the heat is going to break by Tuesday.
[mood:kitchen_practical][shot:establish]Ben, at the kitchen counter, makes himself a sandwich.
Bill returns to the crossword.
Yeah. Thanks, Dad.
I'm not telling you to coach yourself, Ben. I'm telling you what I know. Use it or don't.
Yeah. I'll mention it.
Then tell Coach K. Same advice.
Coach Dale doesn't do that, Dad. Coach K does.
If you are. Tell Coach Dale to put you in the rotation for the second-half conditioning. The first-half guys get tired. Second-half guys get the points.
Bill returns to the crossword.
Okay.
I think so. Coach K hasn't said. But I think so. The half-line work this week was good. The cone work is where he wants it. I think I'm at TE-1.
Ben thinks a beat.
You think you're starting?
[shot:closeup bill]Bill, by the small Bill-tradition he has been doing all summer when the conversation about football has had to happen, looks up from the crossword.
Yeah.
Depth chart up at noon?
Yeah.
Vinton.
Light. They're easing us off for tomorrow.
How was conditioning.

Bill is, by Bill tradition, doing the Friday crossword in pen. His mother is, by the angle of the bedroom door from the hallway, in the bedroom — the night-shift sleep, the eight-AM-to-three-PM sleep she does on days she works a ten-hour straight night. Daisy, the family's twelve-year-old golden, is at Bill's feet.
[shot:closeup bill]Bill is at the kitchen table with the Sentinel.
He goes in through the garage.

His mother's car is in the driveway. The garage is open. His father's truck is on the street, where Bill parks on Fridays because the trash trucks come Friday afternoons and Bill has been parking on the street for the trash trucks since 2014.
He pulls into the driveway at eleven fifty-two.
[mood:day_bright]The drive home is fifteen minutes.
[beat:still]The night holds.
The cicadas, outside, eventually fall.
[shot:insert radio~]The radio, on the windowsill, stays off.
The house, for both of them, is quiet.
She sleeps.
She gets into bed.

Outside, on the porch, Linda Caldwell wakes at ten oh-six. She is, briefly, confused. Then she remembers — porch, granddaughter at the shop, soup in the kitchen — and she stands up slowly, at the careful pace a woman moves at when her hip is healed but she does not yet take the healed-ness for granted. She walks inside. She finds the bed turned back. She smiles in the private way she has been smiling, this summer, when she finds the evidence of her granddaughter's presence in the house.
She sleeps.
She thinks, tomorrow.
[shot:closeup maya]She lies on her back and looks at the pale yellow ceiling.
She gets into bed.
She undresses.
She goes to her own room.
She turns back the covers.

She passes her grandmother's bedroom door, which is open because her grandmother is on the porch. She goes inside and turns back the covers on her grandmother's bed so that when her grandmother comes inside in twenty minutes — which her grandmother will, having been woken by the cooler air or the cicadas or her own internal clock — the bed will be ready.
She climbs the stairs.
She turns off the kitchen light.
She locks the front door.
She goes inside.
She gets up.
She watches it for a few minutes.
The cul-de-sac is quiet.
[shot:establish]She sits in the second chair in the dark.
She turns off the porch light.
She goes back inside. She gets the small light blanket from the back of the couch. She comes back to the porch. She drapes the blanket over her grandmother.
Maya stands in the doorway watching her grandmother breathe — the small steady rhythm of a woman who has, this summer, finally been allowed to rest.
[shot:closeup linda]Linda is asleep in the wicker.
She comes back out to the porch.
She makes a sandwich. She eats it at the kitchen counter. She drinks a glass of water.
She goes inside.
She kisses her grandmother on the forehead.
Maya gets up at ten oh-three.

The cicadas are loud. The cedar smell, off the route Maya rode home on, is faint on her clothes. The iced tea in the second glass has, by the warmth of the night, condensed about half its outer surface into a small ring on the small table.
[shot:establish~]The two of them sit on the porch in the quiet of a Tuesday at nine forty-eight PM.
Good girl.
Yeah.
Yes. That is the right shape of carrying. Holding is, often, what we are asked to do. The doing is rarer than the holding. Most of what we are asked to do, in life, is to hold.
Linda nods.

I am carrying it. I haven't, today, done anything with it. I think tomorrow I will not do anything with it either. The doing — the doing might come next week. Or it might not. The thing might be a thing I just hold for her until she has the next part of it figured out.
Maya thinks.
[shot:closeup maya]Sweetheart. I am not asking what she told you. I am asking how you are carrying it.
Maya looks at her.
And what Wren told you.
Yeah, Grandma.

Yes. He is the kind of man who, when something else is hard, holds onto the work harder. The work is the constant. The work is the thing he can do when everything else is harder than he can manage. Let him do the work. Don't try to make him talk about what is hard. He will, when he is ready, talk about it. Until then the work is the kindness you give him by letting him do it.
He is doing the work.
Maya thinks.
How is Curtis doing.
The two of them sit on the porch for a long minute.
Maya drinks her iced tea.

There are a lot of things, sweetheart, that you don't know. Some of them you will learn this summer. Some of them you will learn later. Some of them you will learn after I am gone. The order of the learning is not for me to arrange. I just answer when you ask.
I didn't know.
Maya is quiet.

Sweetheart, Rick's father was one of those partners. Rick was twelve when he first came into the office. I gave him a stack of bookkeeping ledgers to look at while his father had a meeting. He read the ledgers for two hours. He asked me, at the end of those two hours, what the ledgers were. I told him. He nodded. He came back the next week. By the time he was sixteen he was helping me with the filing on Saturdays. By the time he was twenty he had decided not to be an accountant. By the time he was twenty-five he had opened the comic shop with the money his uncle left him. I have known Rick Pelfrey for forty-nine years, sweetheart. He is the longest professional relationship of my life.
Her grandmother smiles.
You knew Rick before you worked for him?

Honey. I worked for forty-one years at the office of a small accounting firm in New Auburn. Three partners. One assistant — me. The partners changed every fifteen years or so, the way partners do. The assistants did not change. I was the assistant. I watched four generations of partners come and go. The good ones had the staying. They stayed for the work, not for the title. The bad ones came in, hated the work, performed for the title, and left when the title stopped performing for them. By my third year I could tell, on a partner's first day, whether they were a stay-er or a leave-er. By my fifteenth year I had started telling Rick when his clients were going to be one or the other. By my thirtieth year I had stopped having to tell him because by then I had taught him to see it.
[shot:closeup linda]Her grandmother thinks for a moment.
You learned things from somebody about this. Where did you learn it from.
Yeah.
Grandma.
Maya thinks about this.

Curtis is a good man. Most of the men who have worked at small shops for nineteen years are. The ones who aren't, leave. Curtis stayed. You can trust the staying, even when the man is, in a given week, a little raw. The staying is the data.
Yeah, Grandma.
Sweetheart.
Her grandmother does not, while Maya is talking, interrupt.
Her grandmother listens.

She tells her grandmother about Delia from Diamond. She tells her about Wren's hair. She tells her, briefly, about the shape of the thing with Curtis — without naming it as a shape, just the fact that Wren had said something at lunch and Curtis had said something at close and that the day had, in its quiet way, been about being trusted with a thing she had not, until this morning, been entrusted with at this scale.
[shot:establish]Maya sits in the second porch chair.
Sit. Tell me.
It was good, Grandma. It was fine.
How was the shop, sweetheart.
Her grandmother looks up.
Maya parks the bike.

The porch light is on. Linda is in the wicker chair — the one she has been in every evening this week, at the careful pace of a seventy-one-year-old whose hip is healed but who does not yet take the healed-ness for granted — with a glass of iced tea on the small table beside her and a paperback in her lap that she has, by the look of the page, read maybe twelve pages of in the past hour.
[mood:night][shot:closeup linda]Her grandmother is on the porch.
She rides the last three blocks.
She puts the phone back in her bag.
good kid. see you wednesday morning.

how was the rest of the day?

She checks it at the next stop.
[shot:insert phone]At a stoplight three blocks from her grandmother's house, her phone buzzes.
She rides.

The light at nine PM in mid-August is the lavender Texas does in the small window between the day's heat dropping off and the night's full dark settling. The cicadas are loud. The cedar scrub on the route she takes has, in the past two months, become her route — she has been taking it because the main road is busier at this hour and because the cedar route gives her the interior twenty minutes of moving through air without anybody else's voice in it.
[mood:dusk]The ride home is twenty-three minutes.
Me too.

The not-doing is the price of the telling.

dialogue.text: She walks to her bike at the rack.
She goes out the back door. She locks it. She tests the deadbolt. She tests it again.

[shot:establish]She locks the front door. She turns the OPEN sign to CLOSED. She does the walk to the back. She turns off the front fluorescents. She turns off the back-office computer. She picks up her bag from under the desk. She turns off the back-office light.
That is, today, what she can do.

She is going to keep doing her job. She is going to let Curtis keep doing his. At the end of the week Rick is going to come back and the shape of the thing is going to be the same shape it was before, except with one more person — her — knowing what the shape is.
Curtis is going to be okay. The week is going to be okay.

Curtis has just told her, in three sentences, more than he has ever told her. He told her by deciding to mention it. He told her he had registered Wren's lunch conversation with her, that he had a guess as to what it had been about, and that he wanted her to know that whatever it had been about was not her problem. He told her, in his way, that he is on her side. He gave her the assurance an adult gives a kid when the adult has decided the kid does not need to be carrying the adult's problem for the adult.
[shot:closeup maya]Maya, alone in the shop, stands at the counter for a long minute.
The bell chimes.
Curtis leaves.
Good kid.
Curtis nods.
Curtis. I know.
Maya looks at him.
Wren — Wren told you stuff at lunch. I saw her face. I — I want you to know. Whatever she told you, it's — it's not your problem. I want you to know that.
He turns.
He goes to the door.
He picks up his stuff.
Don't make it a thing.
Curtis. Thank you.
She had not, in the day, expected this.
She blinks.
[beat:lift]You're doing fine, kid.
[shot:closeup curtis]He looks at her for a beat that is, she registers, not the beat of his ordinary closing-time pause. The beat is one syllable longer than usual.
Yeah.
Maya.
He pauses briefly.
Thanks, Curtis.
He puts the folder on the counter.
Done.
He comes out of the back office. He has his thermos and his Sentinel. He has the green folder with the Friday invoice now timestamped and filed.
Curtis finishes at eight forty-one.
She waits.
Curtis is at the desk in the back office. The light is on. He is, by the sound of the keys, doing the invoice in the QuickBooks file Rick has been running since 2003.
She comes back to the counter at eight twenty-seven.

[mood:dusk][shot:insert till]Maya, at the counter, starts the close. She counts the till. She separates the cash from the card receipts. She runs the register report. She pulls the bag-and-board waste from the bin under the register. She wipes the counter. She turns off the back fluorescents in sections, leaving the front bank for last. She does the walk-through of the aisles — her own walk-through, which she has been doing without being asked for two months — to make sure the shelves are face-front and the displays are square. The walk-through is not in Rick's notebook. It is a thing she has been doing because she has noticed, doing it, that the morning is easier when the close-night has been thorough.
Curtis goes to the back to run the Friday invoice through.
By eight oh-eight the shop is empty.
The customer at the new-arrivals shelf nods. The two in the back issues say yeah, gimme a sec.
Last call in five.
The shop, at eight oh-one, has three customers left — two in the back issues, one at the new-arrivals shelf.
Wren leaves. The bell chimes.
I will.
Maya. Text me if anything weird happens.
Wren laughs. She picks up her bag. She crosses to the door. She turns at the door.
I always behave.
Curtis. Behave.
I'm good.
You good?
Yeah.
Curtis. I'm out. Big day Wednesday. Maya, you closing?
At seven fifty-eight Wren comes out from the back.
She rings up the next customer.
She does not, in the moment, do anything with the relief.

The exchange has been, on its surface, transactional. The exchange has also been — Maya registers, with the careful attention Wren had three hours earlier equipped her for — a man checking whether the kid running the shop has been entrusted with the paper part of the operation or only the floor part. Curtis has, in asking, confirmed for himself that Rick has not given Maya the invoice.
He returns to the indie rack.
Okay. I'll run it through tonight before I leave.
Curtis nods, slowly.
He didn't write it down. He said it Sunday at noon. He said Curtis will run the Friday invoice through, he knows the schedule.
She thinks. She had read the notebook list four times. The Diamond invoice from Friday is not, she is fairly sure, in the list.
Did he write that down.
Curtis is silent for a beat.
He said you would handle it.
[shot:closeup curtis]The Diamond invoice from last Friday. The one that came in just before Rick left. The one that's sitting on the desk in the green folder. Did Rick tell you what to do with it.
She turns.
Maya.
At six forty-one Curtis comes back out.
Maya, at the counter, has the front of the shop.
He goes to the back office. He sits at the desk. He drinks from the thermos. He reads the Sentinel.
Curtis takes his second break at six twenty-two.
She files the not-glowing along with everything else she has filed today.
She does not know whether this means anything.

Maya has, every time she has been in the back office, looked at it. The red speaker grille is dim. The crack in the lower-left corner of the housing is the same crack it has been since 2014. The Speak & Spell today is just a Speak & Spell.
It has not glowed all day.
[shot:insert speak_and_spell~]The Speak & Spell, on the shelf in the back office, does not glow.

By six the shop has the late-afternoon hum of a small shop on a Tuesday — three customers browsing, two at the back issues, one at the manga wall. Curtis is at the counter. Wren is in the back unboxing a mid-week order from a small-press distributor that is not Diamond. Maya is at the indie rack putting up the new-arrivals shelf-talkers.
She greets the customer who comes in. She wishes them well when they leave.
She receipts.
She rings.
She bags.

By three the shop has had nine customers. By four-thirty, fourteen. By six, twenty-one. Maya, at the register, finds — between customers — that her hands have begun to know the motions of the register and the bag and the receipt without her conscious attention, and that the lack of conscious attention is freeing the part of her interior that has been, all morning, vigilant about being watched by Curtis.
The afternoon is busier than the morning.
She goes back to the floor.
She gets up.

Maya stays in the back office for a minute. She sits at the desk. She does not, in the minute, do anything with what Wren has told her. She files it. She is going to file it again, in different drawers, over the course of the rest of the day and the rest of the week and the rest of the next month. The first filing is the one in the back office at one fifty-three PM with the door open and Curtis at the register thirty feet away.
She goes back to the floor.
She opens the back-office door.
She gets off the desk.
Me too.
Wren. I'm glad you told me. I'm sorry.
Thank you, Maya.
Yeah.
He might guess. Curtis guesses. If he asks you about my face, tell him I had a thing on the phone this morning. Don't tell him what the thing was.
I won't tell him.
Curtis doesn't know.
Okay.

I'm okay. Liz is okay. The thing is — the thing is in motion. The thing will be in motion for a while. By the time Rick is back I will have a better answer than I do today. I am telling you today because today is the day I needed to tell somebody and you are the person who is here.
Are you —
Yeah. Me too.
Wren. I'm sorry.
[beat:still]Wren tells Maya the thing.
Wren takes a breath.
Okay.
Maya looks at her.

I am about to tell you something I have not told anybody else who works here. I am telling you because I think you need to know it for the week. I am also telling you because you have been, since June, the kind of kid who I have decided I would tell things to. I want you to know that you can not, after I tell you, do anything with it. The not-doing is the price of the telling.
Yeah.
Maya.
[shot:closeup wren]Wren sits on the edge of the desk.
Wren closes the door.
The back office is small. The desk is small. The file cabinet is small. The Speak & Spell is on the shelf above the file cabinet, dim.
At one forty-eight Curtis comes back. He goes behind the counter. He takes over. Wren takes Maya to the back office.

Maya and Wren run the floor together for the half-hour Curtis is gone. The floor is steady — five customers in the half-hour, all regulars, none with anything weird. Wren rings. Maya bags. The two of them work the way they had been working since June, when Wren had been first to learn that Maya was actually competent at the register and had stopped, after week two, doing the rings herself when they overlapped.
Curtis takes his lunch at one fifteen. He goes to the small Salvadoran place across the strip mall. He is back at one forty-eight.
Wren nods.
Yeah.
Not a — not a thing-thing. Just a thing. Tell you at three when Curtis takes his break.
Yeah?
Hey. Lunch later. I want to talk to you about a thing.
Wren takes her bag to the small employee cubby behind the counter. She comes back out.
Okay.
That's Curtis behaving. He's a good guy. Just — he gets weird when Rick is out. He'll loosen up by Thursday.
Curtis is being Curtis.
Curtis behaving?
I'm good.
You good, kid? First day solo?
Wren looks at her.
Yeah.
That sounds like Rick.
Wren laughs, short.
I'm okay this week. Rick said you'd ask. He told me to say yes. He said he forgot to tell you.
Okay. I — thank you. I can — I can pick up an extra shift this week if you need. Wednesday or Thursday.
Wren exhales.
Yes.
Maya, who had been told by Rick to say yes, says: "Yes."
Saturday. I — Rick said it would be okay. I'm going to San Marcos. It's Liz's birthday. I want to go down Friday night, come back Sunday. Are you — is that okay?
Yeah.
Maya. Quick thing.
Wren goes behind the counter. She drops her bag. She looks at the register screen the same way Curtis had at ten fifteen.
Yeah.
Cool. I did it last night. I needed — I needed to do something with my hands.
Yeah.
Yeah?
Hair's great.
Morning, Maya. Hair okay?

[shot:closeup wren]Wren is twenty-eight. Wren has, this morning, dyed the front section of her hair a pale lavender Maya had not seen yesterday afternoon when she had left her shift. Wren is wearing the canvas overshirt she always wears, which has, on the back, a faded patch from a band Maya has heard of but has never listened to — Bratmobile, Olympia, 1991 — that Wren had sewn on herself and that has, in the years since, become the thing Wren is most reliably identifiable by from a distance.
Wren arrives at one PM.
She gets up. She goes back to the front to give Curtis his lunch break.
The interior thing is fine. The not-having-anybody is — for today, for the next two hours — fine.
She does not have anybody to be proud to. The pride is an interior thing she is holding by herself at twelve twenty-two.
[shot:closeup maya]She is, she registers, slightly proud of herself.

She has, in the past two hours, fielded a delivery call from a thirty-year veteran of comics distribution who treated her like an adult. She has been part of the invisible network of comic-shop logistics that runs underneath every shop in the country. She is inside it now. Not because of Frasier. Not because of any of that. Because Rick is in Dallas, and Delia called the number she was given, and Maya picked up the phone.
She sits at the desk.

She does not, immediately, tell Curtis the truck is going to be late. She does not need to. Curtis will, by his own clock, have already factored in that the truck is sometimes Wednesday, and Curtis does not like being told things he has already factored.
Maya finishes her sandwich.
Delia hangs up.
I'll tell him.
You tell him Delia says hi. Tell him I said the boxes are heavier this month. He's gonna want to send the strong one out to the truck.
Yeah.
Rick at the con?
I'm Maya. I'm Rick's — I'm covering for Rick this week.
You're new. Are you the new —
Yeah. Thanks for letting me know.
Honey, just a heads-up. Driver's running behind. Could be Tuesday very late, could be Wednesday morning. Sign-out window's nine to five, you know the drill?

It is Diamond Distribution. The dispatcher is a woman named Delia, who Maya has not spoken to before but who introduces herself with the efficient warmth of a person who has been doing distribution dispatch for thirty years.
[shot:insert phone]The phone rings.
She eats her sandwich at the desk at twelve fourteen.

Sammy. Nothing. I — I want you to know what I did and why I did it. I want you to be able to make your own decisions about what part of me, going forward, you keep. I do not — I do not want you to forgive me. Not on a timeline. I want you to be able to say, when you are forty-five, my dad did some things I have to figure out how to think about, and he tried, in the end, to be honest about them. That is — that is what I want. The forgiveness — the forgiveness is your business. I am not going to ask for it.
He looks at her.
What do you want from me.
Yeah.
Dad.
Okay.
Sam nods.

Some. Not all. She knew the favors existed. She — she has, over the years, asked enough questions to learn the shape, even when I declined to tell her the contents. She has, I think, known longer than she has said. Wednesday night I told her everything. Everything I am telling you now and the long version. She listened. She did not — she did not ask me to make any decisions about what to do. She let me make them. That was — that was, Sammy, the most generous thing she has ever done for me. I do not know if I deserved it. She gave it anyway.
He thinks for a moment.
What did Mom know.
Yeah.
Dad.
The lake makes its small lake sounds.
A long silence.

Wednesday morning. After dinner Tuesday — when I — when I told you about the safe deposit box — I went to my office and I sat for an hour. I had had, that day, the message that the Ramos boy was being moved up. I had had — it doesn't matter. I sat for an hour. I thought about what — I thought about what kind of man I would be, in five years, if I made the move he wanted me to make Wednesday. I thought about your mother. I thought about you. I thought about Ken Brower in the parking lot in 2016, and how Ken had, by 2016, been a man I would not have, at twenty, recognized as a man I was willing to become. I — I made the decision. I called Hernando Ramirez at one AM. He did not seem surprised. He told me to come in Friday morning. I did.
When did you — when did you decide.
Sam is silent.

I was going to spend the next twenty minutes trying to explain to you how the man I have been working for is — strange — without sounding like a crazy person. You have just told me you already know. So I am going to skip that part. I am going to tell you, instead, the part that is harder for me, which is: I knew. I knew he was strange. I knew the favors were — wrong. I did them anyway. I told myself, every year, that I was doing them for you. I told myself I was doing them for the mortgage. I told myself I was doing them so we could afford the things you had. I told myself I was — managing. I was not managing, Sammy. I was — I was being managed. I want you to understand the difference. I did not, until this past week, fully understand the difference.
He drinks his coffee.
Okay, Sammy. That makes — that makes some things easier to tell you.
Okay.
[shot:closeup miller~]Her father exhales — a long careful exhale.
Maya's grandmother. Her grandfather, too. He took a picture in Graustark in the seventies. D. Dean cost him fifteen years. He is — Dad, he is not new. He is old. Whatever he is.
Sammy. How.
He looks at her for a long moment.
I know who D. Dean is.
He looks at her.
Dad.
[mood:arcana_cool][shot:closeup sam]Sam, on the dock, is very still.

By 2019 the favors had — they had grown. By 2021 I was making — choices — about whether specific kids stayed in town. Kids who had — kids who had drawn the wrong attention. Whose parents had drawn the wrong attention. By 2023 I was — I was doing what I did this past week. Or a version of it. With — with the Ramos boy this past Saturday I was — I was told about him, in the same conversation Ken had been told about people in 2007, at the same parking lot, by the man I have, since 2018, been dealing with. The man's name is Dean. D. Dean. I do not know what the D stands for. I have asked. He has never told me. He is — Sammy. I want you to understand. He is not a normal man. He is — he is the kind of man whose presence in a room you cannot, after the meeting, fully describe. He is — he was older than me when I met him in 2017 and he has not, in nine years, gotten older. I do not know what to do with that fact. I have, for nine years, declined to think about that fact.
He pauses.

The first one was small, Sammy. It was — it was a man named Kowalski. Not — not Ben's family. Different Kowalski. Older man. He had been complaining at HOA meetings about the substation. They asked me to — to handle it. Handle meant, in this case, to make sure Mr. Kowalski's rental property ran into a series of code violations that prevented him from renewing his lease. I — I did it. He left town within six weeks. I told myself, at the time, that he was a difficult man. I told myself it was just paperwork. I told myself many things.
What was it.

Ken died in September of 2016. Heart attack. He was sixty-one. NexCorp came to me — a man in a suit, not the man I have been dealing with this past year, an earlier man — and offered me Chief. He offered me three things. One: a forty percent raise. Two: the same payroll arrangement, with NexCorp covering the PSA's books. Three: he said, very quietly, that there would be — favors — that I would be asked to perform from time to time, and that I would be told what they were when they came up, and that I would be told I had a choice but that the choice would not, practically, be a choice. He said this to me in the parking lot of the substation on Gallatin at eleven PM on a Thursday. I drove home. I sat in the driveway for two hours. I went inside. Your mother asked what was wrong. I told her — I told her about the raise. I did not tell her about the favors. I took the job. The first favor came in March of 2017.
He pauses.

Before I made Chief — that was the year I made Chief, in October. Before that, I was a deputy. The PSA was — different then. Smaller. The Chief at the time was a man named Ken Brower. Ken had been doing the job since the subdivision opened. He had — he had an understanding with NexCorp Residential Solutions. The understanding was, the PSA looked the other way on certain — operations — that took place inside the subdivision in exchange for two things. One: NexCorp covered the PSA's payroll, which the city of New Auburn had been threatening, every two years, to cut. Two: NexCorp made specific people — certain specific people — disappear in ways that did not look like disappearances. I want you to understand that I am, this morning, simplifying. The actual arrangement was complicated. There were — there were forms. There were — there were other agencies, other names. But that is, in essence, what it was.
She does not, immediately, react.
[beat:hit]I started in 2016.
[shot:closeup miller]He breathes.
He drinks. He sets the cup down on the wood between them.
She pours coffee for both of them.
He hands her the thermos.

[shot:insert dock]They walk to the dock — the same dock, she registers, that he is talking about, which is, twelve years on, the same wood, very slightly more weathered, with the same metal cleat at the far end where she had, at six, decided cleats were boring and had returned to the Cheez-It box. They walk to the end of the dock. They sit on the edge with their feet over the water, the way you sit on docks when you do not, on this particular morning, plan to fish.
She gets out of the truck.
He gets out of the truck.
He nods.
Yes, Dad.

I want to tell you some things. Not all the things. Most of them are going to come out tomorrow at the arraignment, or in the discovery, or in the — the stuff that's going to happen over the next year. I am not going to make you sit through the whole list this morning. But there are some things I want to be the one to tell you, before a lawyer or a reporter or a man in a suit gets to. Is that okay.
He pauses.
You wouldn't. You were five. But I remember it. I have remembered it every time I have driven up here since.
I don't remember that.
Sam laughs, briefly.

Sammy. I want to do this here because — because this was the first place I ever brought you outside the subdivision. You were five. I had — I had taken the day off because your mother was sick and you were being a handful. I brought you up here. We didn't fish. We sat on the dock and ate Cheez-Its out of a box. You told me, that morning, that when you grew up you wanted to be a quote librarian or a hawk.
He does not, immediately, get out.
He parks.
[shot:insert truck]Her father pulls into the lot near the north boat ramp.

The lake has been quiet since the Sinkhole, technically — Lake Palestine is far enough north of the New Auburn corridor that the water has not, since the Calamity, registered any of the chemical changes the Gulf-side reservoirs have. But the lake is quiet in a deeper way than that, this morning, because it is Sunday at six-thirty in late May and because most of the bass fishermen who would normally be out have not yet, at this hour, finished their pre-dawn coffee.
[mood:day_bright]The lake is quiet.

[mood:morning_bright][shot:establish~]The kitchen, in the small bright way kitchens do this work, becomes the room where the next chapter of Maya's life is, without her quite registering it, beginning to be set.
Anita laughs.
Bill snorts.
I will tell her about Daisy at length.
Gracie nods solemnly.
It would help me, actually. If she's awake she'll want to know about — about people. Gracie can tell her about Daisy.
I want to.
Gracie, sweetheart, you don't have to —
Yes.
[shot:closeup gracie]Gracie's face does, for an instant, the small unguarded thing eleven-year-olds' faces do when they have been invited to a thing they had not, dared, ask for.
Want to come to the hospital with me?
Yeah.
Gracie.
Maya, halfway through the second egg, looks up.

Gracie watches her eat with the unembarrassed curiosity of an eleven-year-old who has, this morning, decided that Maya is the most interesting thing to ever happen to her family's kitchen and is going to need, going forward, to be observed at all meals.
The eggs are perfect.
She eats.
Bill.
Bill.

dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr. Kowalski.
Hot sauce is in the cabinet to the left of the stove if you want it.

dialogue.text: [mood:kitchen_practical][shot:insert eggs]Bill brings over a plate. Two eggs over-easy, two pieces of toast, a strip of bacon. He sets it in front of Maya without comment.
Anita.
Anita.
Thank you, Mrs. Kowalski.
Maya looks at her.

I called the hospital at seven. Your grandmother is awake. She is asking for you. They moved her up to the third floor at five-forty. Room three eighteen. Visiting hours are nine to nine. I can drive you over after breakfast.
[shot:insert phone]Anita slides her phone across the table.
She sits at the table next to Anita. Daisy comes out from under the table and puts her head on Maya's foot. Maya rubs Daisy with her toes.
Yeah. Eggs would be amazing. Thank you.
Maya laughs.
You are wearing my mom's shirt and it looks like a dress on you.
How'd you sleep, sweetheart.
When Maya comes in, all four of them look up, in different registers.

[shot:closeup bill]Ben's father — Bill, fifty-one, water-plant operator, broad-chested in a way Ben has clearly inherited — is at the stove cooking eggs. Anita is at the table in scrubs, still up from her shift, drinking coffee. Gracie is at the counter eating cereal in her pajamas. Daisy the dog is under the table.
[shot:establish]The kitchen is full.
She goes upstairs.
Maya gets up. She washes her face. She uses the bathroom. She puts on the t-shirt and jeans Anita has left on the chair, which, as advertised, swim on her.

The basement is, as Ben had promised, a real bedroom with a real door. It has a small high window through which the morning light comes in low and yellow. The bed is a queen with a quilt that Maya does not recognize, and the quilt smells faintly of lavender, in the way of quilts kept in linen closets that women like Anita Kowalski maintain with a small specific ritual every other Sunday.
[mood:morning_bright]Maya wakes up in the basement.
Morning, Maya. Eggs?

Thomas worked for the Beaumont Enterprise for two years out of college, then quit to freelance. He shot mostly architecture and event work — weddings, school portraits, the occasional industrial commission. In 1976 he was hired by a company called Ardent Reclamation Holdings to document a chemical dump site outside Graustark. The site had been listed for cleanup. The company wanted before-and-after photographs. It was, in his understanding, a public-relations contract.
Okay.
I want to. I have wanted to for forty-eight years. I have not, until now, had the right person to tell.
Grandma. You don't have to.

[mood:arcana_cool][shot:closeup linda~]Your grandfather. Thomas. I told you he took a picture in Graustark in the seventies. I told you it cost him fifteen years. I want to tell you what the picture was.
Maya nods.
I've been thinking, since I woke up. I want to tell you some things while I have the strength to. I'm going to be okay. The doctor said three weeks. But I want to use the morning.
Maya sits.
Maya. Sit.
[shot:establish]Linda and Maya are alone.
The door closes.
She gestures Gracie. Gracie, reluctantly, follows.
Linda. We're going to step out for a few minutes. Let you and Maya have a moment. We'll be in the cafeteria. Maya, take your time.
She has the best instincts.
Daisy has good instincts.
Linda laughs.

Daisy is a mutt. Daisy is technically a coward. She is afraid of butterflies and ceiling fans and the vacuum. But she is brave about people. She is very brave about Maya. She slept on Maya's foot at breakfast which is something she only does for people she has decided to keep.
[shot:closeup gracie]Gracie comes around to the side of the bed. Gracie sits on the visitor's chair, which is too large for her. She leans forward.
Gracie. Tell me about Daisy.
Nothing to thank me for, ma'am. We're glad to have her.
Anita. Thank you. Bless you.
Linda smiles.

This is Anita Kowalski. She's Ben's mother. They are taking care of me until you come home. This is Gracie. She is Ben's little sister. She has a dog named Daisy. She would like to tell you about Daisy.
Maya straightens. She gestures.
I'm here. I'm here, sweetheart. Sit. Tell me about the people in this room.
Grandma.
I'm sorry I scared you, baby.
Linda strokes Maya's hair with the IV hand, gently, ignoring the IV.

[shot:insert hands]She does not, immediately, embrace her grandmother — Linda's hip will not, this week, tolerate embraces — but she takes Linda's free hand in both of hers and holds it, and she puts her forehead against the back of her grandmother's hand, and she stays that way for maybe twenty seconds.
Maya goes to the bed.
Sweetheart.
When Maya comes through the door, with Anita and Gracie behind her, Linda's whole face changes.

She has, in the night, been moved from recovery to the regular floor. Her hip is in a brace and a cast. She has an IV in her right hand, which is the hand she would, normally, use for the Morse key, and she has noticed this and has, in her quiet way, registered the irony.
[mood:fluorescent_corridor][shot:closeup linda]Linda Caldwell is sitting up.
There are seventy-six days left.
The summer will continue.
The town will, in its small ways, begin to learn what it is, after a Saturday that did not kill any of them and a Monday that did not, against expectation, take her father from her.
The week will close.
They will, both of them, sleep.
They will not, that night, talk about it.
They will sit at the table for a long time after.
They will eat together.
Sam's mother will, without comment, set the third plate.
There will be enough for three.
But the house, when they walk through the door, will smell of the cooking her mother had started before they left. Pot roast. The same one, cooking all afternoon on warm.
The house, for the first time in nine years, will be — formally, on paper — a house her father does not, today, live in.
They will go inside.
Her mother will, gently, wake her.
Sam will, by the time they reach the driveway at four-fifty-one PM, fall asleep in the back seat.
The third wheel was the older system, deciding, on its own quiet schedule, that this family was, today, going to get a ride home.
The third wheel was Miriam.
The Chariot, drawn by two horses pulling in opposite directions, has — for one quiet hour at the close of one strange Monday — found its third wheel.

Sam, in the green Subaru, headed home, eats a small bag of pretzels Miriam offers her from the glove compartment, and watches the freeway, and feels — for the first time in a week — the small clean settling of a load that has been, for some time, distributed across the entire upper half of her body, beginning at last to come down into the chair beneath her.
Outside, in the New Auburn afternoon, the sun does its slow late-May work.
The hum hums.
She says, quietly, to nobody and everybody: Thomas. The girl is at the courthouse. She did fine. The room's friend brought the car. The mother held the hand. We are going to be alright, love.
She closes her eyes.
Linda smiles, very faintly.

In Room 318 of New Auburn General, Linda Caldwell turns on the small bedside radio that Anita has, before leaving with Gracie at noon, plugged in for her. The radio is not the shortwave at home. It is a hospital radio. It picks up, on its preset stations, the New Auburn AM news loop, the Tejano station out of San Antonio, and — on a frequency that should not, by any FCC allocation, exist — a faint patient hum on what the dial reads as approximately 1776 kHz, between two assigned bands.
They drive home.
Miriam puts the Subaru in gear.
She rests, for a moment, in the same place that the girl from Maya's story had rested, six weeks ago, on a different leg of the same long route.
She gets in the back seat.
She does not say it aloud.
Nicola. Aria. The third one.
Twilight-colored.

[shot:insert quilt]But the seat itself — Sam can see, with the small attention that has, this week, become her practice — bears, on the upholstery, a single faint outline of a quilt that has been, recently and for a long stretch, folded there.
The back seat is empty.
She looks at the back seat.

Sam, looking at the car as she approaches it, recognizes — with the small quiet click of a piece settling into a slot it had been built for — that she has, in some sense, seen this car before. In a story Maya had told her on Tuesday, in the back room of Cosmic Comics, about a silver-haired woman and a dark green wagon and a girl in the back seat heading west, six weeks ago, through New Mexico.

[shot:insert subaru]The green car is, when they reach the curb, a 2009 Subaru wagon, dark green, immaculate, with a silver-haired woman at the wheel who is, at this exact moment, reading a paperback copy of Princess Mononoke: The Art Of and smoking — though she will, when they approach, immediately stub out the cigarette and apologize, bad habit, I've been working on it.
He walks them out.
I think that's right, Mary.
Hernando. We're going to take the green car.
Sam, her mother, and Ramirez stand for another long moment.
She turns. She walks out.
I have a car at the curb. I can give you a ride home. It's the green one. Let me know.
Miriam. Thank you.

Mary, Sam. I am Miriam. I am — I'm a friend of friends. I won't intrude long. I just wanted to tell you in person: he's going to be okay. Where he's going is — it isn't pretty, but it isn't punitive. He's going to be doing the federal thing. He'll be in touch within a month, in writing, from a routed address. You won't be able to write back at first. By next year you will. By Christmas next year, probably, you'll be able to see him.
Miriam crosses the aisle.
[shot:establish]Sam, her mother, and Detective Ramirez stand together in the gallery, not moving.
The courtroom rises and disperses.
He leaves through the main doors.
The man in the charcoal suit, in the second row of the prosecution side, gathers his folders. He stands. He does not, at any point, look at Sam.
Across the aisle, Miriam gives her another small unworried smile.
Her mother, beside her, presses her hand once.
She lets her hand fall.
I will, today, only have to feel that he is alive and that the room is, in its strange way, on his side.
I will, in the next year, learn how to feel about this.

Whatever he is going to be, in the next five years or ten or however many, he is going to be alive. He is going to be a witness. He is going to be in a place I do not know the address of. He is going to come home, eventually. Or I am going to be told, eventually, where to go. The older system, today, has chosen to keep him.
He knows.
Her father does not, technically, see it. The door has closed.
[shot:closeup sam~]Sam, in the third row, raises her own right hand to her own neck.

Sam's father is, at 15:04, escorted out the side door — by federal marshals, not by state deputies. He does not, on the way out, look at the gallery. But just before the door closes behind him, he raises his right hand to the back of his neck in the small specific gesture Sam knows from her childhood — the gesture he had made when she was small and he was leaving for a long shift. I love you. Be back when I can.
The lawyers confer.
Counsel. Logistics.
dialogue.voice_name: Cameo - Calm and Soothing American Narrator for Explainers & Audiobooks

dialogue.text: Yes, your honor.

The court has accepted your plea on all eleven counts. The court has also received and reviewed an emergency motion filed by an interested party requesting an alternative custodial arrangement pending federal proceedings. The court is, at this time, deferring sentencing to a date no earlier than ninety days from today, pending the outcome of the federal proceeding referenced in the motion. You will be remanded to federal custody pending the outcome of that proceeding. You are, at this time, technically a federal witness rather than a state convict, although your state plea stands. Do you understand.
dialogue.voice_name: Cameo - Calm and Soothing American Narrator for Explainers & Audiobooks

dialogue.text: Sam's father stands.
[mood:studio][shot:establish]Mr. Miller. Please rise.
