dialogue.text: She takes the bench.
Judge Halverson returns at 14:54.
The recess continues.
Sam's mother, who does not know who Miriam is and who has already, in the past four hours, stopped being surprised by anything, returns the gesture.

Miriam, who has been, by Sam's mother's hand-pressure on Sam's hand at the moment Sam noticed her, already noticed by Sam's mother, raises one hand off her lap in the universal small gesture of I am here. You don't have to know me yet. I am here.
Miriam smiles, small and unworried.
Miriam, across the aisle, meets Sam's eye.

I will be okay because the people in the gallery on my side now include my mother, Detective Ramirez, four friends my own age, three additional adults I have, this past week, met, my grandmother on my mother's side from beyond the grave, and — she now realizes, looking at the third row of the gallery directly across the aisle from her own row, where a silver-haired woman in a gray wool coat has, at some point during the recess, quietly seated herself — at least one woman she has never met but whose face she now recognizes from Maya's description of Miriam.
Dad will choose. I will be okay with whatever he chooses.

The older system has its reasons. The older system has been running my father since 2017 and is, today, offering my father an exit. The older system is not, in any human sense, on a side. The older system is, in some sense, the chessboard, and the chessboard is, today, rearranging itself in a way I am not equipped, at seventeen, to understand.

She has seen him before. Not in a hallway. At 03:03 on Wednesday, in the dream she wrote down one minute later: her father at twenty-something, in a uniform she did not recognize, shaking hands with a man in a charcoal suit whose eyes found hers because the dream was not a record but an attention. The notebook is at home. The handwriting still says what it says.
He does not, this time, look up.
He is, again, reading a folder.
[shot:closeup sam]Sam, in the third row, looks at the man in the charcoal suit.

Mary. I think — I think Dean might also be the man who is, inside the federal apparatus, the one running this investigation. I think — I think he is on multiple sides of this at once. I think he has been, for some time.
Ramirez looks at her.
Hernando. Dean is the bad guy. Mike just told Sammy yesterday morning, at the lake, that Dean is the man he has been working for since 2017.

Yeah. Mary. I don't — I don't know what he is. I have never, in twenty-two years, been in a room with him. The folder he filed is real. The federal docket is real. The investigation he's referring to is — it's real. I called a friend in the marshals during the recess. There is, in fact, an open federal investigation that requires Mike's cooperation. The witness-protection offer is — it's standard, in those cases. It's not a trick, on its face.
Hernando. Dean is offering this.
Sam's mother stares at him.

Mary. Mike's plea has been — accepted. The charges are not changing. What Dean has filed is — Dean has filed a request with the court that Mike be permitted to enter what's essentially a witness-protection program in lieu of a custodial sentence. Dean is offering — or his organization is offering — to relocate the family, to provide ongoing security, in exchange for Mike's continued cooperation on a federal investigation that is, apparently, larger than this one.
Ramirez sits down.
Ramirez comes back.

He gets up. He goes to the front. He confers, briefly, with Ana. He confers, briefly, with the prosecutor. He confers, after a long moment, with the man in the charcoal suit, who answers him with a small calm courtesy that — Sam can see, even from the third row — does not change.
I don't know. I don't know what's in that folder. Give me twenty minutes.
Hernando.

The bailiffs ask the gallery to remain seated. The defense lawyer — Ana Rivera — turns and looks at Sam's mother. Her face does the specific thing a lawyer's face does when something unexpected has happened that has not, yet, been characterized.
She stands.
Mr. Dean. I am — I am going to take a brief recess to confer with counsel. Bailiff — please ask the gallery to remain seated. We will reconvene in twenty minutes.
dialogue.voice_name: Cameo - Calm and Soothing American Narrator for Explainers & Audiobooks

dialogue.text: The judge, after a long minute, looks up.
The courtroom is very quiet.
She reads.
The judge opens the folder.
[shot:insert folder]He hands the judge a folder.

He does not, Sam notes, walk like the men around him. He walks the way the man in her dream had walked — without hurry, without exaggerated patience, with the small specific economy of a person who has, in some sense, already arrived everywhere he is currently going.
Dean walks to the bench.
Approach.
dialogue.voice_name: Cameo - Calm and Soothing American Narrator for Explainers & Audiobooks

dialogue.text: She puts them back on.
Judge Halverson takes her glasses off.
Your honor. The amendment is on the docket. Filed at ten forty-six.
The clerk, beside the judge, looks at her screen.
I am, your honor. By the second amended docket filed this morning at ten forty-six, I am listed as an interested party with rights to address the court at the arraignment. I have the documentation.
Sir. You are not party to this proceeding.
dialogue.voice_name: Cameo - Calm and Soothing American Narrator for Explainers & Audiobooks

dialogue.text: Judge Halverson looks at him.
Your honor. May I approach.
The bailiff at the door of the gallery looks at him.
[mood:arcana_cool][shot:closeup dean]But before she finishes the sentence, the man in the charcoal suit — D. Dean — stands up.
She is going to say per the standard sixty-day calendar. She is going to give the date. The date is going to be in late July. Sam and her mother are going to sit through it.
Counsel. The court accepts the plea. Sentencing will be scheduled per —
dialogue.voice_name: Cameo - Calm and Soothing American Narrator for Explainers & Audiobooks

dialogue.text: Judge Halverson nods.
There is a small sound from the gallery — a stir, the sound a courtroom makes when it has just been told a thing it had been expecting to be made to wait for.

The defense — Sam's father's lawyer, a woman named Ana Rivera, calm, fifty-something, who had been the lawyer Ramirez had brought up from Houston for the Friday morning intake — enters a plea of guilty on all eleven counts.

The prosecution lists the charges. The list is — the list is longer than Sam had let herself imagine. There are eleven counts. They are, in summary: official misconduct. Multiple. Conspiracy to commit kidnapping. Multiple. Conspiracy to defraud the public. Aggravated. Failure to act on multiple federal mandatory reports. The federal counts are, the prosecutor notes, going to be filed separately by a federal prosecutor in a different proceeding.
The arraignment proceeds with the small specific tedium of arraignments.
Sam, in the third row, watches the back of his head.
He has accepted this counsel.

He has been told — Ramirez had told him at six AM — not to look at his daughter during the proceedings. Ramirez had explained: Mike, the press in the back row will see the look. The look will be the photograph. You don't want her face to be the photograph. Wait until afterward.
He does not, in the moment of being seated, look at the gallery.
He sits at the defense table beside the lawyer Ramirez had arranged.

He is in his civilian clothes — the gray slacks her mother had laid out this morning, the white shirt, no tie. His hands are not cuffed. He has, Ramirez had explained at six AM, agreed to a self-surrender arrangement that did not involve cuffs as long as he was cooperating, which he is, fully, intending to do. He looks, in the courtroom light, smaller than Sam had ever seen him.
[shot:closeup miller]Sam's father is brought in from the side door.
The clerk reads the docket.

The judge is a woman Sam has never heard of — Judge Patricia Halverson, sixty-something, NAUC bench since 2006, with the small patient expression of a judge who has, over twenty years, learned that the best thing she can do for the dignity of her courtroom is to be unimpressed by everyone in it equally.
At 14:31 the judge enters.
Okay.
Her mother's hand tightens.
That's Dean.
Sammy. Who is that.
[mood:studio][shot:closeup mrs_miller]Sam's mother, who has felt the small change in Sam's hand, says, very quietly:
He returns to his folder.
He does, in time, look away first.
She does not look away.
The eyes are — Sam realizes — exactly the eyes from the dream she had on Tuesday night, at three AM, the dream she had written down and then folded into the back of her notebook.
He looks up, briefly, when Sam looks at him. His eyes meet hers across the room.
He is reading a manila folder.
[beat:chill][mood:arcana_cool][shot:closeup dean~]In the second row, behind the prosecution table, there is a man in a charcoal suit.

The room is — Sam registers, with the small steady attention she has been doing for ten days now — bigger than she had expected. The ceilings are higher. The wood is darker. The smell is of old varnish and the specific brand of carpet shampoo that municipal facilities have been using since the nineteen-eighties. There are — Sam counts — twelve other people in the gallery besides her group. Three of them look like reporters. Two of them look like NexCorp lawyers — she does not, technically, recognize them as NexCorp lawyers, but they are, as a category, recognizable. The rest are unidentifiable.
Sam looks around the courtroom.
Sam's mother has, since pulling out of the driveway at one PM, not let go of it.
Sam's mother holds Sam's hand.

Ramirez sits in his civilian clothes. Khakis, a dark polo, the rain jacket folded on his lap. He is, Sam has noticed in the four hours she has now spent in his presence, a man who occupies a chair the way a man occupies a chair when he has spent twenty years occupying chairs in courtrooms — without slumping, without performing alertness, with the small steady patience of a person who is aware that the room's center of gravity will, in a moment, shift, and who intends to be where he needs to be when it does.

Ramirez is not, technically, here in any official capacity. Ramirez is here because he asked to be, and because Sam's mother — who had only met Ramirez for the first time at six AM today when he had come by the house to drive her father to the courthouse — had, after meeting him, asked him to be.
[shot:establish]Sam is in the third row, with her mother on her left and Detective Ramirez on her right.

It does not, as is usual, start at two PM. The judge is finishing lunch. The bailiffs are coordinating with the holding deputies. The attorneys are at the long pew at the front, going through a stack of folders that arrived this morning at eleven and that nobody, until eleven, had been told would be the size that they were.
[mood:studio]The arraignment is set for two PM.
The shift is, today, easy. The shift is, today, just a shift.
Then she goes back into the Kwik Stop. She finishes her break. She works her shift.
[shot:establish]Sam sits in the car for another five minutes.
They hang up.
Thank you.
Yes.
Graciela.

Diego asked about your father, mija. I told him your father turned himself in yesterday. Diego cried. He cried because he had been afraid your father had — I will not say it. I will say only: Diego cried because he had been afraid for you, even in there. Even in the room they kept him in. He had been carrying you, mija. He had been carrying the worry about you. Now he can put it down.
Graciela. Tell him. Tell him I love him. Tell him he should not have been carrying me. Tell him I have been carrying him too. Tell him — tell him Monday.
I will, mija.
[shot:closeup sam~]Sam, in her Corolla in the parking lot of the Kwik Stop where she had come, on her break, to take this call in private, sits with the phone against her ear and weeps quietly.
Diego asked about you again this morning. He asked twice. He asked when he could see you. The doctor said Monday, maybe Tuesday. Diego said Monday. The doctor said we will see how Diego feels.

She is telling Sam, in the slow careful way she tells things, what Diego has — between sleep and water and his mother — said about the five days. Not the worst of it. Graciela is, herself, learning the worst of it as Diego comes back to himself, and is choosing carefully which pieces to relay to Sam. The pieces she is relaying are the ones that will, in Graciela's judgment, give Sam what Sam needs to know without giving her what Sam does not yet need to carry.

The safehouse is, by Hal's protocol — agreed upon Friday night with the doctor and the grandmother and Doyle — open today only to family. Diego's mother arrived at six-thirty this morning from San Antonio. She is, at this moment, in the bedroom with Diego, who is sitting up for the first time, drinking water, looking at her, talking, slowly, in Spanish, about nothing in particular.
[shot:closeup graciela]Outside, on the porch, Diego's grandmother — Graciela Ramos, who has not left the safehouse since arriving last night at ten — is on the phone.
She has been talking with Sam for forty minutes.
She is on the phone with Sam.
[mood:day_bright]Sam, Maya, and Jesse are not at the safehouse.
Mija. Always.
Yes.
[shot:establish]They eat.
Lydia brings the food.
Yeah. Me too.
We're all lucky in this group. I'm — I'm starting to figure that out.
You're a good kid, Ben. Jesse's lucky.
[shot:closeup eileen]She smiles at him for the first time.
Yes ma'am — Eileen.
Thank you.
Yes.
Ben looks at her.

Okay. One thing I want from you. Not from Jesse — from you. I want you to be the one who comes to the house tonight. I am going to call Jesse home from his shift at six. I am going to make dinner. I am going to keep dinner warm. We are going to wait for Jim to come out of the darkroom. When he does, you and Jesse and I are going to sit with him. Will you do that.
Eileen nods.
Step three is — I do not have step three yet. I think step three is whatever the answer to step two is. I think we get one and two right first.
Step three.

Step two is — there is a man in Graustark named Frasier Temple. He runs — he runs digital things. Imps. He has been watching this town through them. He is the one who has been telling us things. He may know what is using your husband. I can ask Maya to ask him. If he knows, we will know.
Step two.

Step one is — you and Jesse and I sit down with Mr. Henderson when he comes out of the darkroom. We do not confront. We do not press. We let him talk if he wants to. We sit in the kitchen with him. We eat. If he wants to write things, we give him a pen. If he wants the lights off, we turn them off. If he wants to sit in silence, we sit. The note on the bill — I will come back when I can — that means he is, sometimes, coming back. Our job is to be there when he comes back.
Ben thinks.
You're the ones who have a plan, Ben. I'm the one who has fourteen months of evidence and no plan. You and I are going to figure out what we do. Tell me what your group thinks the next step is.
Eileen. We're seventeen.
Ben blinks.
Now. Tell me what you and the kids think we should do.
She drinks her coffee.

Don't be sorry, Ben. Be glad. I have been alone with this. I am no longer alone with this. That is what your sentence has done. That is what your friend Jesse has done. That is what my husband, by writing what he wrote on that bill, has done.
Eileen. I'm sorry.
[shot:closeup ben]Ben does not, for a moment, know what to say.

I have not shown the list to anyone. I have not told my husband I keep it. I have, for fourteen months, been waiting for someone to come to me with a sentence that would let me believe my list. You have, this morning, given me the sentence.
She pauses.

I've known something was wrong with Jim for fourteen months. I have not, until now, had a name for it. I started keeping a list of things at the same time you started keeping yours. Mine is in a steno pad in the top drawer of my sewing table, behind a jar of buttons. The list is small. It has fourteen items. Item one is, October 2024 — pupils contract irregularly under bright light. Item two is, November — won't sleep more than three hours at a stretch. Item three is, December — has begun referring to the darkroom as 'down there' instead of 'the darkroom.' And so on. Item fourteen, this past Tuesday, is referred to himself, while half-asleep, as 'the eye.'
Okay.

Ben. I want to tell you something. I want you to hear it carefully and I want you to file it, because I think you and I are about to be on the same side of a thing for some time, and I want you to know what you're working with.
She is quiet.
Eileen. Yes.
Eileen.
Yes ma'am.
Okay. So you four kids.
She nods slowly.
Yes.
Maya Daigle. Linda Caldwell's granddaughter.
Yes.
Sam Miller. The chief's daughter.
She opens them.
[shot:closeup eileen]Eileen closes her eyes for a long moment.

Because — Eileen, this is not — this is not the only thing happening in the town this week. There has been a — there has been a kid taken. Diego Ramos. He is, as of yesterday evening, safe. We — Jesse, me, Sam Miller, Maya Daigle — we have been on it. The adults handled the rescue, but we have been holding the information. We needed to wait until the rescue was done before we could tell anybody anything new. I'm — I'm sorry. We needed Friday to happen first.
And you waited until today to tell me because —
She nods.
Since Monday afternoon.
How long have you known.
Since Sunday.
How long has Jesse known.
With the photographs? Per Jesse — since at least the start of May. Maybe earlier.
How long has this been going on.
[shot:closeup eileen]Eileen wraps her hands around her coffee cup.
Lydia arrives with the coffee. They both pause. Lydia pours. Lydia leaves.

The third is — your husband is fighting it. Whatever it is. I don't know what it is. I don't know how it works. But Jesse and I both think the note on the bill is — was — your husband telling us he is trying to come back from where it has put him. We think he came in here on Wednesday because he was trying. We think he wrote the note knowing one of us would read it. We think the note is — Eileen, I think the note is the thing he could get out before whatever's using him made him stop.
And the third.

Jesse and I have, between us, identified two of the people. One of them is a man in a charcoal suit who, in the photograph, is looking directly at the camera. Neither of us knows him. The other is a small figure — four feet tall, in a wide hat, holding a hand-rolled cigarette — that I cannot, in good conscience, ask you to take seriously, and which I am asking you to take seriously anyway.
She does not, immediately, say anything.
She looks at him.

Second. Jesse has, since Sunday, been finding photographs in your husband's darkroom. Eight-by-ten prints. Photographs of locations in town — the Gas & Go, Meadowlark Circle, the front entrance of the subdivision. The photographs have, in them, people. Specific people. The negatives Jesse has checked do not show those people. The prints do.
Okay. Second.
She reads the note three more times. Then she folds the bill back along the existing creases. She puts it in her purse. She puts the purse on the bench beside her.
Her face still does not move.
[mood:macro_haze][shot:insert bill~]The red light lies. I am sorry. I will come back when I can.
She reads it.
She unfolds it.
You don't have to read it now.
[shot:insert bill]He takes the bill out of his front pocket. It has been folded in thirds for three days. The fold is precise. He sets it on the table between them, fold up.
On the back of the bill, in pencil, in handwriting I now know to be his — Jesse confirmed yesterday — there was a note.
Okay.
Eileen's face does not move.

Three things. The first is the easiest. Your husband came in here on Wednesday at eleven-fifteen. He sat in this booth for forty-one minutes. He did not order anything. Lydia tried twice. He said no thank you both times. He looked, the entire time, like a man who was trying to decide whether to come back into the kitchen and say something to me. He did not come back. He left at eleven fifty-six. He left a ten-dollar bill on the table.
Ben takes a long breath.
She waits.
Eileen. Yes.
Eileen.
Yes ma'am.
Okay. You said over text last night you needed to talk to me about Jim.
Eileen looks at Ben.

A waitress — Lydia, who has been at the Pit Stop nine years, who does not, in any visible way, register that this booth is anything other than a regular Saturday-morning breakfast — comes over. She takes their order. Eileen orders the egg-white scramble and a coffee. Ben orders the short stack and a coffee. Lydia leaves.

Jesse is on shift. Jesse is, deliberately, not at the front of house. Jesse is in the kitchen with the morning prep, where he has agreed, with Ben at six AM by text, to stay until Ben taps the bell on the pass-through twice — twice means come out, once means stay back. Jesse has agreed to this because he trusts Ben. He also agreed to it because he has, in the eight days since Diego went missing, been finding that there is a small specific peace in being told what to do by someone whose attention he has begun to trust. He is in the kitchen now, doing the eggs.
He sits.
Sit, Ben. You don't need to stand for me.
Eileen.
Eileen, please.
Mrs. Henderson. Thank you for coming.

[shot:closeup eileen]He stands when she comes through the door. He does not, unlike most of the Pit Stop's regulars, give the small overfamiliar diner-greeting Brenda has trained the front-of-house staff to give. He simply waits at the booth until she crosses the floor, and then he says, in the small steady voice he has been working into all morning:
Ben is at the booth when she arrives.

[mood:day_bright]The back booth at the Pit Stop is the corner one, three from the kitchen, with a window that looks out on the strip-mall parking lot and the Coin Wash next door. It is the booth where, on Wednesday, Mr. Henderson had sat for forty-one minutes without ordering. It is also the booth where Eileen Henderson, this morning, is going to sit for forty-one minutes — though she will, this time, order, and she will, this time, eat, and she will, this time, by the end of the meal, be a different woman than the one who walked in.
The week, somehow — against pressure, against every reasonable expectation — has not killed any of them.
The summer continues.
The town hums.
Diego and his mother, at the safehouse, both asleep in the same bed.
Ben and Maya, in two rooms of the same house, both, finally, asleep.
Sam, in her cornflower blue bedroom, asleep, with her father's text from ten minutes ago — love you, Sammy. tomorrow we drive to the lake. early. bring a jacket. — face-up on her dresser.
Maya and her grandmother, across the city, tethered by a phone line that is not, at this hour, ringing.
Eileen and Jim, on the couch.

The Lovers card, in some other deck on some other table, would tonight have been showing — for the first time in many printings — both figures clothed, which is how the card sometimes prints when its meaning is not, this week, about romance, but about the deeper choice the Lovers also represent: the choice to remain in the same room as the other person, and to keep being two, on purpose, against pressure.
He goes back to work.
He sits at his workbench. He looks at the silver-spoon riverboat in its glass case. He thinks, Linda. Good for you, kid.

In a warehouse in Graustark, Frasier Temple — alerted by his Demons at twelve fourteen AM Central — stands at the door of his cathedral for the first time in some months, looks out at the dark of the parking lot, considers, briefly, walking to his car, and decides — after a long minute — to go back inside.

In the Henderson house, Mr. Henderson is on the couch in the living room with his wife, who has not, this evening, been able to bring herself to leave him alone in their bed and who, instead, has decided they are sleeping out here, together, with the lamp on, until the new arrangement settles.

In a hospital recovery room, Linda Caldwell sleeps the patient sleep of a woman who has just, for the first time in thirty-seven years, allowed her own body to fail — and who is, in the failure, also being permitted, for the first time in thirty-seven years, to rest.
In Maya's grandmother's house, three blocks away, the shortwave radio sits dark, untouched, for the first night in five days.
Outside, the Texas night does its small late-Saturday work.

His mother sits at the table for another hour, in her scrubs, until her husband comes home from the late shift at the water plant smelling of chlorine, and they sit together at the kitchen table, and they talk quietly, and they decide, between the two of them, that whatever Ben tells them this week, they are going to believe him.
He goes upstairs to bed.
He hugs her.
Good.
She is, Ma. She's okay. They both are.
Go to bed. I'm going to wait up for your dad. He's still at work. He's going to want to know the kid is okay.
She nods.
Yeah, Ma.
You're going to tell me even if it scares me.
Yeah.
You're going to tell me everything.
Yeah. I know.
You're going to need to tell me what's going on. Not tonight. In the next couple of days.
Yeah, Ma.
Ben.
His mother looks at him.
Ben stays in the kitchen.
[shot:establish]Maya goes downstairs.
Maya nods.
Anita. Please.
Thank you, Mrs. Kowalski.
Maya looks at her.

[mood:kitchen_practical][shot:closeup anita]Sweetheart. There's a bed downstairs. There's a glass of water on the nightstand. There are clean clothes on the chair, my old t-shirt, you'll swim in it, that's fine. Bathroom is at the bottom of the stairs. We'll talk in the morning. Sleep.
What she says, when Maya comes through the door, is:

Ben's mother has, in the time since, made up the bed in the basement. Ben's mother has, in the time since, set out a clean towel and a toothbrush still in its package. Ben's mother has, in the time since, decided what she is going to say to Maya when Maya comes through the door.

The Kowalski house, when they arrive, is dark except for the kitchen light. Ben's mother is at the table. Ben's mother is in her scrubs. Ben's mother had been called by Ben's father at eleven, and Ben's father had said Linda Caldwell broke her hip and our boy is at the hospital with her granddaughter and I think we are going to need to have a conversation.
Ben drives her.
Maya, who has not slept, agrees to come home with Ben for a few hours.
The surgeon comes out at twelve-twenty-eight AM. The surgery has gone well. Mrs. Caldwell is in recovery. She will be moved to a regular room in the morning. Maya will be able to see her at six.
[shot:establish]They sit in the waiting room for another forty minutes.
Okay.
Okay.
She exhales.
I am sure.
Yeah.
Maya.
Are you sure.
Maya is quiet for a moment.

Maya. My mom is a nurse. She works nights. My dad will say yes. Gracie will lose her mind. The dog likes you. I have a basement. There's a real bedroom down there with a real door. It's three weeks. We're inside the same school district. We have the room. Stay at my house.
Ben —
[shot:closeup ben]Stay at my house.
Ben thinks for half a second.
I — I don't know. I haven't — the social worker came down. I told her I have a friend. I — I do not, technically, have a guardian alternate listed.
A pause.
Where are you going to stay while she's in rehab.
Yeah.
Maya.
I know.

She is going to be in a rehab facility for three weeks and then she is going to come home and you are going to make her tea every afternoon and she is going to teach you the Morse and you are going to sit with her at the radio and she is going to be okay.
I know.
She is not going to die.
I know.
Maya. Letting it down is what she was supposed to do.

[shot:closeup maya~]She has been carrying this for thirty-seven years. Since 1989. Since my grandfather. She has — she has been holding it for thirty-seven years. And then I came, and then this week happened, and she — she let it down. She let it down enough to fall.
Yeah.
She fell because she was tired.
Yeah.
Ben.
Okay.
She's — she's going to be okay. They said the surgery is straightforward. She's seventy-one but she's strong. They said three weeks in rehab. Then home.
I know.
He didn't know it would be her.
Yeah.
F.T. was right.
[shot:closeup maya]After a long minute, Maya says, very quietly:
Ben does not move.
After a moment, Maya leans her head against his shoulder.
He does not, immediately, say anything.
He sits beside her.
Ben crosses the room.

[shot:insert coffee]She is in a chair against the back wall. She has, on her lap, a paper cup of coffee from the vending machine that she has not drunk. She is, when Ben comes through the door, very small.
[mood:fluorescent_corridor]Maya is in the waiting room when Ben arrives.
He eats.
He picks up his fork.
Oh.
[mood:kitchen_practical][shot:insert pot_roast]He looks down at his plate. He looks at the half-eaten roast in front of him.
Yes, love. You have. And it's still warm.
Have I?
You've been eating pot roast for ten minutes, Jim.
She laughs. It is the small wet laugh of a woman who has just, in her own kitchen, gotten her husband back.
Could I — could I have some pot roast.
Yes, Jim.
Eileen.
Yes sir.
You're a good boy, Ben. Thank you for being — thank you for being here.
Yes sir.
Ben.
Yes sir.
You're — you're the diner boy. Jesse's friend.
Mr. Henderson looks at Ben.

Mr. Henderson. There is a man in Graustark named Frasier Temple. He runs — he runs the kind of system that probably knows what was put in your camera. Maya — Maya Daigle, who is one of our — one of our friends — has a way to ask him. We can ask. We can find out what it is. We can find out if it can be — if it can be removed.
[shot:establish]She looks at Ben.
Neither do I. We are going to find out.
I do not — I do not know what kind of help.
Jim. We are going to get you help.

[shot:closeup eileen]Eileen, across the table, is crying — quietly, without sobbing, the way a woman who has been waiting for a confession for fourteen months cries when the confession finally arrives.
I am — Eileen, I am sorry.
He looks at Eileen.
He stops.

And then — Saturday last, I — there was a kid. The Ramos boy. The eye — the eye saw him. The eye — I — I told them where he would be. That night. I told them. And then on Tuesday morning I saw, in the prints, a man in a charcoal suit looking at me. He was not — he was not real. Or he was. I do not — I do not know. But he was — he was seeing me back. And after I saw that — Eileen, after I saw that, I began to — I began to fight. Not on the — not on the surface. On the inside. I would — every print, after, I would try to — to leave a thing. A small thing. The note on the bill. The pencil writing. The eye did not know I was doing it. The eye — the eye thought I was being a good eye. But the small things — they were mine. They were — the only mine I had left.
He pauses.

In April — Eileen — in April this year, the substation began — broadcasting — at me. Through the camera. I do not — I do not know how to explain it. It was not — it was not a voice. It was a — it was a direction. The camera would tell me where to point. The prints would — the prints would report. I was — I was not, by then, fully — fully me. I was — I was an eye. [shake rate=8 level=2]I was only an eye.[/shake] The eye was — the eye was theirs.
Mr. Henderson keeps going. His voice does not change.
Jesse closes his eyes.

Then — Eileen. Then in 2011 — there was a — they put something in the camera. Or in me. I do not know which. After that — I would go down to the darkroom. I would develop the prints. The prints had — they had things in them I had not photographed. I had — I had photographed the same things I had always photographed. But the prints were — they were different. And after — after the prints came out, I would — I would know things. About — about the people in the prints. About where they were. About what they were doing. I — I would tell — I would tell, and they would pay. More, by then. Much more.
He pauses.

It was — for years, it was just photographs. Just — pictures. Of intersections. Of — of houses I did not know. I would — I would take the picture. They would pay me. It was small. It was easy. I told myself it was — I told myself many things.
Eileen does not interrupt.

There was a — there was an arrangement. In 1998. When we were — when we first moved to Harmony Creek. The substation went up the year before. The substation had — had a contract with NexCorp Residential Solutions. The contract was for — for ambient signal management. They needed — Eileen. They needed a small number of — eyes. People with cameras. People with — with a kind of attention. The arrangement was — they would not interfere with our lives. They would only ask, occasionally, for — photographs. Specific photographs. From specific angles. At specific times. They would compensate. Modestly. The compensation was — it paid for the down payment on this house. It paid for Jesse's preschool. It paid for things I was, at the time, unable to pay for any other way. I was — I said yes. I did not — I did not understand what I was saying yes to.
He takes his time.
Take your time, Jim.
[mood:arcana_cool][shot:closeup mr_henderson]I would like to tell you all what happened. I do not know how much of it I can tell. I do not know what I — I want to try.
After perhaps eight minutes, Mr. Henderson sets down his fork.
Mr. Henderson does not look at his son. But he stops chewing for a long second. Then he resumes.
Jesse — who is sitting next to his father, on his right — puts his hand on his father's forearm. Briefly. Once. Then takes it away.
Ben does not, at first, say anything.
Eileen does not, at first, ask him anything.

He eats slowly. He eats one bite at a time. He chews each bite for longer than is strictly necessary, in the way a man chews who has, somewhere in the last forty-eight hours, forgotten that food is something his body is allowed to want.
He eats.
Eat, Jim.
She sits.

She gets up. She gets the pot roast from the oven. She sets it on the table. She gets the carrots and the potatoes and the small dish of horseradish her husband, since 1999, has put on his pot roast. She sets it all down.
Eileen does not, immediately, respond.
I'm — I'm back.
He breathes.
He puts his hands flat on the table.
[shot:establish]He sits.
Please.
Can I — can I sit.
I did.
Eileen. Did you make pot roast.
He looks at the fourth chair.
He looks at the table.
He looks at Ben.
He looks at Jesse.
Mr. Henderson looks at her.
Hey, Jim.
His eyes — Ben sees, and Eileen sees, and Jesse, who has been watching for this most carefully, sees first — his pupils contract normally.
His eyes adjust to the kitchen light.

He looks — Ben registers, with the small specific attention he has been training all spring — like a man who has not slept in two days and who has, in those two days, been somewhere very far from his own kitchen and is, this evening, only just returning to it.
[shot:closeup mr_henderson]Mr. Henderson comes through the doorway.

[shot:closeup sam~]The Emperor is stepping down on Monday and I am going to be there when he does.
Saturday.
Monday.
Friday.

[shot:insert phone]She takes out her phone. She texts Ben: home. She texts Maya: home. She texts Jesse: home. She gets, within four minutes, three replies: home, home, home. She puts the phone down. She lies on her back on the bed. She watches the ceiling fan. She counts the clicks. Three, six, nine.

[mood:night][shot:establish]Sam sits on her bed. Outside, the rain has stopped entirely. The Texas night is doing its post-storm thing — the cicadas tuning up, the mockingbirds confused by the sudden change of pressure, the small far-off hum of the substation that Sam has, all her life, not heard and that she is, this week, starting to.
Her mother cries, quietly, for about ten seconds. Then she stops. She kisses Sam on the forehead. She says, "I'm proud of you." She gets up. She leaves Sam's room. She closes the door behind her.
I said I will come. I love him. I don't like him right now but I love him. He's my dad.
Sammy, you don't have to —
[shot:closeup sam]I will come to the arraignment.

I am going to stand by him. We have talked about it. We agreed. I am not going to leave him. I want you to know that separately from his decision, because you are seventeen, and you get to make your own.
Sam does not, immediately, speak.

He wanted me to tell you three things. I'm going to tell you them. One. He loves you. He has loved you every second of your life including the seconds he was doing the bad things. He wants you to understand the two facts do not cancel each other. Two. He is asking you, for Monday, if you will come to the arraignment if it happens on Monday afternoon. Not to support him. Just to be there. He does not expect you to and will not be angry if you refuse. But he is asking. Three. The blue tin in his sock drawer also has, inside it, a letter to you that he has been updating over the years. It is in a manila envelope. He is asking you not to read it until — until he's gone to wherever he goes after Monday. I don't know when that is. He thinks it might be six, seven years. Maybe ten. It depends on what he can plead to.
Sam stares at her.

[beat:hit][shot:closeup mrs_miller]Your father has, tomorrow morning, agreed to meet with Detective Ramirez at the NAPD substation at seven AM. He is going to give Ramirez a — everything he has. What he knows. Who he knows. What he's done. Everything. This is not a negotiation. This is him making a full statement with a lawyer. Ramirez has agreed to keep him out of custody through the weekend so he can see the — the rescue thing, which I am not supposed to know about but which I know about, through. He will be arrested Monday morning.
Her mother takes her hand.
Okay.
Your father is downstairs in his office. He'll be up in a bit. I want to tell you something first, alone, because I didn't get to tell you enough of it last night.
Sam sits.
Sammy, sit.
Yeah. It was good.
Did you have a good time.
Hey, Mom.
Hey, Sammy.

[mood:candlelight_low]In the kitchen at 1428 Meadowlark, Sam comes home to a house that is, for the first time in some years, completely dark except for the small under-cabinet light her mother leaves on when her mother is awake upstairs. Sam goes up. Her bedroom door is open. Her mother is sitting on her bed.
[mood:dusk][shot:insert truck]They walk to the curb. Ben's truck. Bench seat. Four people. It is tight. It smells of grease and Mountain Dew and old Pit Stop french fries.
Okay. Truck, ten minutes, as agreed.
Jesse, Sam, Maya, and Ben stay back. Jesse pulls the garage door down halfway so the four of them can stand in the opening and talk.

The band takes a break. At nine-oh-six the band resumes. They play one more song — a cover, Pixies' Here Comes Your Man, which Jesse's version is not quite right but which is, in Jesse's version, exactly right for a garage on a Thursday in late May. At nine-thirty, the band packs up. Nate, Carl, and Em leave first.
Thanks, Jesse. For — yeah. Thanks.
Thanks, Sam. For asking.
[shot:establish]The song ends. Carl twirls his stick.

[shot:closeup sam~]Sam, on the camping chair, does not cry. She does not, she realizes, need to cry. The four lines fall into her chest in the specific way good lyrics fall into a person's chest when the person hears them at the only moment in their life that they will ever, exactly, mean. She mouths the last line under her breath. Ben, watching her, notes it. Maya, on her chair, has her head tipped back against the workbench, her eyes closed.

[beat:lift][shot:establish]They play Blowback. The chorus is — even Jesse will later admit — the thing that makes the song. The chorus is four lines. It goes: There is a door / The door is not locked / We have not, yet, tried / The handle.
Okay. Sam. For you.
I'll pick it up.
dialogue.voice_name: Shannon B - Sad Emo Teenage Girl

dialogue.text: Em?
Yep.
Carl?
Of course.
You remember Blowback.
Jesse is quiet for a moment.
The chorus. I've always liked the chorus.
Sam shrugs, small.
Why.
Yeah.
Blowback.
Jesse looks at her.

[mood:candlelight_low][shot:closeup sam]Sam, without thinking about it, says: "Blowback." Blowback is Jesse's band's second-oldest original. Jesse has not played it in four months because he has decided, quietly, that the song is not good. Sam has not, in her life, requested Blowback.
So. Sam, Maya, Ben. You have a request? You guys came to hear something.

The band eats. The four teenagers and the three band members eat. The Telecaster is set aside. Nate has taken his bass off. Carl has come out from behind the kit and is sitting on the floor with his back against the amp. Em has the last slice of the gluten-free side because Carl has, as he does every practice, politely offered her more than his actual need.
Eileen Henderson leaves the pizza. She ducks back under the door. The door closes behind her.
Thanks, Mom.
Hi, sweetie. I'm glad you came. Jess, baby, there's garlic knots too but I left them inside. Come up in a sec if you want them.
Hi, ma'am. I'm Maya.
— welcome. I've met Sam. I'm Eileen. Ben, Jesse's told me about you. Maya —
Here she gestures at Sam and Ben and Maya with a small wave that is, Ben notes, more careful than her usual.

I know. Plates. Napkins. Eat. Nate, do not spill. Carl, your mother called me twice to make sure I was going to remember about your gluten thing — this pizza is half gluten-free, the side closest to the door. Em, your mother says hi. Kids —
Mom, you're a hero.
Carl hits the crash once, theatrically, and the band stops.
Pizza! Pause for pizza!
It is Jesse's mother, ducking under the partially opened door with a pizza box balanced on her hip and a stack of paper plates in the other hand.

At eight-seventeen the garage door rumbles. All three of them — Sam, Maya, Ben — tense. The band continues playing. They have not, with the volume of Grid Failure at this point, heard the door. The door opens two feet, then pauses. It is not Chief Miller. It is not Mr. Henderson.

Ben has been keeping a mental ledger of the emotional weather of the group. He has not, yet, written any of it in the legal pad. He is not sure whether the ledger belongs in the legal pad. He is beginning to suspect that it does not — that the ledger is for him, privately, as the thing he does with the attention he has been cultivating for the past three months, now that the attention has, at last, become about people rather than cars.
Sam Miller laughed. First time since Sunday. The laugh was in response to Maya, in a garage, during practice. Note: this, also, is data.
Sam laughs. It is the first time Sam has laughed in five days. Ben, across the two chairs, hears the laugh. Ben does not react externally.
That's a sentence, Sam.
I have been in this garage maybe ten times in my life. This is the first time it has felt like a garage and not, you know. A chief's house's garage.

The band is on their third run-through of Grid Failure. Em has started harmonizing above Jesse's lead, a third interval that she had not tried before and that, when it lands on the downbeat of the chorus, makes Nate turn his head — the universal bassist's gesture for that is new and I approve.

The song is loud. The song is, in Jesse's garage, on a Thursday evening in late May after a thunderstorm, exactly what the three on the workbench need. Sam feels her shoulders drop two inches. Maya closes her eyes. Ben leans back against the garage wall and, for the first time in forty-one hours, does not think about cars.

The band launches into the song they had been working on for a month. It is called Grid Failure. It is, as far as Jesse has written the lyrics, about a specific kind of failure of a specific kind of electrical grid, but the lyrics are — Jesse will admit, privately, later — not especially good. The song is mostly riff. The riff is: distorted Telecaster doing a three-chord ascending figure over a driving eighth-note bass and a snare that hits on the and of two and four. Em's backing vocal is a long sustained syllable — ohhhh — that sits under the chord changes like a drone.
Jesse, at the mic, is doing the small pre-practice check he always does — one two one two, Carl you ready, Em ready, okay count it. Carl counts it: one, two, three, four —

They converge. They set up. They tune. There is the usual bickering about the snare head and the usual low-grade tuning conflict between the bass and the Telecaster and Carl's usual joke about the Christmas lights, which Carl has made every practice since November and which everyone laughs at anyway. Sam and Maya and Ben sit on the workbench, then on the camping chairs Jesse pulls out from under the workbench, and drink warm Mountain Dew from the cooler Nate has brought, and watch.

The band arrives in a staggered burst over the next four minutes. Nate — the bassist, seventeen, a skateboarder whose hair has, this month, been dyed the specific green of a traffic-light go. Carl — the drummer, sixteen, smaller than the rest of them, wiry, with a nervous laugh and a left-handed kit that he has, over the past year, almost — almost — taught himself to play right-handed. Em — the backing vocalist and occasional keyboardist, eighteen, three inches taller than anybody in the garage, with a small specific I am from Fort Worth energy that Jesse has always, quietly, admired.
Cool. Okay. Uh. This is them.
I know Carl. He comes into the Pit Stop on weekends.
I don't know any of them.
I know Nate from Algebra.
Come in. Pizza's on the way. Nate and Carl and Em will be here any minute. You guys know them?

Sam hugs him. Sam does not, generally, hug Jesse. Sam and Jesse have been in the same friend orbit since ninth grade, have sat at the same lunch table for two years, have, on some occasions, watched movies on the same couch, but have not, in Sam's memory, been huggers of each other. Sam hugs him anyway. Jesse hugs back. Briefly, firmly, with the small surprised gratitude of someone who has just discovered a category his friend group has been refusing to occupy and has, tonight, entered. Ben shakes Jesse's hand. Maya — to Ben and Sam's collective small surprise — hugs Jesse too. Maya is not, any of them will later realize, a hugger in her usual register. Maya is here to announce a membership.
Guys.

Jesse, when he sees the three of them coming up the driveway together, makes the small unguarded sound a person makes when a thing he had not, consciously, expected to be given is, in fact, given. He hops off the workbench. He meets them at the door.
[shot:establish]Okay. Let's go in.
Sam looks at him for a long moment.
[shot:closeup ben]Sam. I've been waiting to get to have friends. I had not, until Monday, understood that waiting was over. I am — I am very glad you are my friends. I am doing what I know how to do.
Ben pauses.
Thank you for being like this.
Yeah.
Ben.
Okay.
Okay.

Okay. We go in. We do not talk about any of it in there. Jesse has his band practicing in twenty minutes. The band doesn't know. We do not tell the band. We sit, we watch, we eat whatever pizza Jesse's mom sends down, we leave at nine-thirty. After practice, the four of us talk in my truck for ten minutes. Then we all go home and do not do anything else tonight. Okay?
They stand for a moment.
Yeah.
Tired.
I don't know.
How is everybody.
[shot:establish]The three of them converge at the foot of the driveway. They do not, immediately, go up.
[mood:dusk][shot:closeup ben]We need to get her a ride home tonight.

Sam arrives second. She is in the Corolla. She parks behind Ben's truck. Maya arrives third. She is on her bike, in the rain, with her backpack on and her hair wet. She chains the bike to the light post at the end of the driveway. Ben, watching her through his windshield, winces slightly — Ben has registered that Maya has been on her bike in every weather since April, that Maya is the only one of the four of them without a car, that this is a condition that has not, until this moment, been something the other three have explicitly thought about.

Ben arrives first. He is in his truck. He parks at the curb. He does not pull into the driveway, because the driveway is where Jesse's father parks, and Ben — who has never been inside this house but who has, over the past forty-one hours, begun to build a small careful map of it in his head — does not want to be where Jesse's father would park, on the theory that Jesse's father may come home during practice and that Ben does not want to be the thing Jesse's father sees first.

The garage door is closed against the rain, which has mostly stopped but which has left the subdivision in the specific sticky humidity that follows a Texas storm. The air in the garage smells, faintly, of turpentine and sawdust and cold metal and the Mountain Dew. Jesse sits on the workbench and drinks his Mountain Dew and listens to the rain on the garage roof, which is tapering, and tries — for the first time all day — not to think about his father. He does not, in the end, succeed.

The bill is at the Pit Stop, folded, in Ben's apron pocket. Ben had texted Jesse at eight-oh-seven PM on Wednesday: bill is safe. Jesse had replied: thanks. He had not asked for more. Ben had not offered more. Ben had offered, instead, at seven-fifty PM: do you want me at practice thursday. Jesse had replied, yes. Ben is coming tonight. Ben is also bringing Sam and Maya, because Jesse had, at eleven PM last night, texted all three at once: practice thursday at 7. suburban blight. come if you can. Sam had replied in four minutes: i'll be there. Maya had replied in seven minutes: i don't know music. is that ok. Jesse had replied: maya it's a garage band. nobody knows music. Maya had replied: ok.
[shot:closeup jesse]Jesse sits on the workbench. He is drinking a warm can of Mountain Dew. He is waiting for Nate and Carl and Em. He is, at seven-fourteen, thinking about the ten-dollar bill.

[shot:insert drum_kit]The drum kit is at the back. The amp is against the side wall. The Telecaster is on its stand, unplugged, waiting. The bass — his friend Nate's — leans against the amp. The microphone — which belongs to the band and which lives at the bassist's house when not in use — is plugged into the small mixer Jesse built from a kit in tenth grade. The strobing Christmas lights are plugged in. They strobe.

He swept the garage at five PM because his mother asked him to. He swept it again, without being asked, at six, because the first sweep had missed a small drift of paint chips in the corner by the workbench, and because Jesse has decided — without being able to articulate exactly why — that tonight's practice should take place in a garage that has been swept twice.

[mood:candlelight_low]Jesse has swept the garage. He does not, generally, sweep the garage. His father sweeps the garage, on the first Saturday of each month, with the thoroughness of a man who believes that a floor is a kind of moral statement. Jesse has always, privately, thought of the garage as his father's territory in the same way he has thought of the darkroom as his father's territory. He has not, until this week, swept either one.
[shot:closeup claire~]Better than I'd be. She doesn't know it yet. But better than I'd be.

The reporter — her name is Claire Moyer, she has been with the Chronicle for eleven years, and the work she is currently doing is not on any masthead she would ever be credited under — takes a long breath.
The girl.
The girl?
How's she holding up.
Miller is being told.
Is Miller running it.
Yeah.
Eight days got cut to two.
[shot:closeup claire]They're moving him tonight.
She hangs up. She looks at her partner.
Understood. We're in position.
A pause.
It's early.

[shot:insert phone]The woman picks up her phone. She calls a number that is not in her contacts and that she does not need to dial, because her phone has had the number saved under a name her partner will never ask her about.

[mood:macro_haze][shot:insert sedan]At six-oh-seven, in a white sedan parked at the gravel turnout past the last named road on the east side of the subdivision, a woman in her mid-thirties wearing a HOUSTON CHRONICLE lanyard and a man in his fifties with a fading golf-shirt sunburn exchange a look they have exchanged forty-one times in the past three days. The look does not, externally, convey anything. Internally it conveys: here it starts.

At six-oh-five, the first transformer on Gallatin trips. The power flickers across four blocks. At six-oh-six, the transformer resets itself. The power comes back. Everybody's clocks, except for the microwave at the Kwik Stop which was already nine minutes fast, are now forty-six seconds behind.

The sprinklers, on their schedule, do not run. Wednesdays are off days for the east side of the subdivision. Wednesdays receive the rain the sprinklers would otherwise have provided. The HOA has, in a memo circulated in 2014, described this arrangement as the grid's quiet efficiency.

At six-oh-four the first thunder rolls across the subdivision, deep and sustained in the way thunder rolls when it has been gathering off the Gulf since midnight, and the rain comes down not in the typical Texas way — fast, heavy, gone in twenty minutes — but in the slower more insistent way storms come down when they have decided, for some private reason, to stay a while.

[mood:rain_interior]The thunderstorm arrives early. The weather app on Sam Miller's phone had, as of Tuesday evening, been predicting the first rain at fourteen-oh-eight Wednesday afternoon, with a fifty-three percent chance of hail and a forty-one percent chance of the kind of localized flash flooding that Harmony Creek's engineered drainage system had been designed, in 1997, to render theoretical. The forecast had been wrong by approximately eight hours.

She will, without being able to explain why, put her hand on the counter in the direction of the back office and spread her fingers. The Speak & Spell, through the wall, will fall still. It will, Rick will later confirm, fall still smiling.

The Speak & Spell sits on its shelf, red grille dim, small crack in the corner, quiet. It does not, today, broadcast again. It does, at three PM, faintly hum — on and off — in a rhythm Maya, at the counter, will hear and will recognize as affection.

The bell over the door chimes. A customer comes in. Mrs. Delacroix, mid-sixties, buys a new Archie collection every Wednesday, tips Maya fifty cents each time. Maya resumes her counter face. Rick returns to the office.
Okay.
Okay.
Yeah, kid. I've been meaning to. I have not, yet, figured out how. Maybe you will. You're a Daigle. Your dad had a way of getting into that warehouse. Maybe you will.
Rick smiles — a small tired smile.
Can we — can we help him. Sometime. After this.
She looks at the floor.
Oh.

I don't think so, kiddo. Not entirely. He has been alone in that warehouse for a long time. He has been a friend in a specific narrow way, which is that he watches and he transmits and he keeps the lights on. I have never, in twenty-four years, seen him in person. Not once. I don't think anyone has, in a while. I think he needs more than he's getting. But he's not ready to ask.
Rick. Is Frasier — is he well.
Maya closes her book.
Opinions. Yes. I know how that sounds.
Opinions.

No, kiddo. He knows what he knows about Diego because his imps are, as far as I can figure, eavesdropping on every electronic signal in this subdivision. That is how he knows where Diego is. That is also how he knows your grandmother's radio works. That is also why your browser has started getting F.T. messages. He has been looking out for you through his imps. The imps have opinions. The imps are, apparently, very fond of you.
Does he know Diego.

[shot:closeup rick]His name is Frasier Temple. He lives in a warehouse in Graustark. He has known your dad for a long time. He is a friend. He is a genuinely strange man. He has not, in any way I have ever been able to detect, been anything other than kind to the people he has decided to be kind to. He has decided that about you.
Who is he.
Yeah.
Rick.
I told him you did.
I liked it.
Not me, no. But a friend of mine. He says hi. He says he's sorry it was weird. He says he was trying to be — quote — affectionate.
He pauses.
The Speak & Spell.
Was what me.
Was that you.
Yeah, kiddo.
Rick.
[shot:closeup maya]Maya looks up from her book.
[shot:establish]Rick sits at his desk for a long moment with the phone in his hand. Then he gets up. He goes to the front of the shop.
Click.
Good. I have to go. One of my Demons has decided today is its birthday and is attempting to order a cake. I've got to dissuade it.
I hear you.
Yeah. If any of the wrong kind of men walk into your shop in the next forty-eight hours, you lock the back before they get there. You don't engage. You call the sedan. You hear me.
Rick's hands on the door.

He's alive, Rick. We're going to get him. Tell Maya to hold the map for one more day. They're moving him tonight. We can't intervene tonight — we'd get all of them in the crossfire. We intercept Friday morning, from Zone-G, on the transport out. Sedan people are handling the mechanics. Your job is to keep Maya's head clear and Rick's hands on the door.
Is the kid — is the Ramos kid —
Yeah.
Frasier.
Take care of her for me. And take care of yourself. The storm's going to get worse.
Yeah. I know.
Rick does know why.
Rick. You know why.
Why.
I can't.
Come visit.
I'm okay, Rick. I'm getting older. The cathedral's a lot of building for one guy to run. But I'm okay.
[shot:closeup rick]A long silence. Then Frasier says, in a quieter voice:
Are you okay.
Yeah.
Frasier.
She's not freaked out. She's charmed.
There you go.

[shot:insert mirror]Rick looks through the one-way mirror his long-dead predecessor had installed in 1983 between the office and the sales floor. Maya is at the front counter. She is reading. She has, at this moment, Rick notes, a small sedimentary smile on her face — the smile of a kid who has just, in her own private head, received a piece of news that she finds, despite herself, funny.
Ask her how freaked out she is.
She's going to freak out.

Yeah. I hear you. I'll have a word with them. It was supposed to be text only until next week. But I'd rather them be affectionate with her than ignore her. She's on her grandmother's frequency already. She can take it.
Jesus, Frasier.
Rick, honestly? I didn't. The imps did. I think they like her.
A longer pause. Then the voice — Frasier Temple's voice, which Rick has heard maybe eight times over the past twenty-four years — says:
When did you decide to bring Maya in directly.
I am. The imps are — they developed opinions. We've discussed this.
I thought you were quieter these days.
Yeah, that'll happen.
A small amused exhale on the other end.
Your imp just addressed Maya Daigle through a 1978 Speak & Spell in my back office.
Rick.
A pause.
Joneses.

[panel:off][mood:day_bright][shot:closeup rick]Rick, who has been at his desk for most of the broadcast, sets down the pen he has been holding and picks up his phone. He does not dial F.T. He dials a different number, one he has had saved for nine years, one he does not, himself, fully understand the identity of. The line picks up on the second ring. The voice on the other end is older, male, with the faint distant quality of a voice coming through a bad connection even when the line is clean.
The Speak & Spell falls silent. The grille stops glowing.

Another pause. F. T. says hello. Maya. Hello. Please listen. T. R. I. U. M. V. I. R. A. T. E. Triumvirate. This word is your word. You are becoming a part of it. Three of you in this town. Three more elsewhere. Do not be afraid. You are not the only one.
A pause. Then: T. R. I. U. M. V. I. R. A. T. E. Triumvirate. Correct. Try again.
The grille is glowing, and the Speak & Spell is producing, in its tinny synthesized child-voice, a sequence of letters. T. R. I. U. M. V. I. R. A. T. E. Triumvirate. Correct. Try again.

[panel:vol6_speak_and_spell][shot:insert speak_and_spell~]It is broadcasting now. Its red speaker grille is glowing faintly. Not the ordinary amber of its ordinary LED — a different red, more like the red of the darkroom safelight in Mr. Henderson's converted broom closet across town.

[mood:arcana]Rick is in his office when the Speak & Spell starts. The Speak & Spell has been on the shelf behind his desk for eleven years. It is a 1978 original, battered, with a small crack in the lower left corner of the red plastic housing. It had been given to Rick by a customer in 2014, who had said at the time you seem like the kind of guy who would appreciate something weird, and Rick had laughed and accepted it and had kept it there ever since, sometimes as a paperweight, sometimes as a conversation piece, never, until this morning, as a broadcaster.

[mood:rain_interior][shot:establish]Sam stands at the window for another forty-five seconds. The face does not reappear. The rain keeps coming down. She turns away. She goes to the closet. She gets dressed for work.
Her grandmother on her mother's side had died in 2019.
That was my grandmother.

She blinks. The face is gone. It had been, she realizes with a small slow settling-in, a face she half-recognized. An older woman. Dark hair going silver. Kind eyes. A face that was not, in any way Sam could articulate, frightening.

[mood:arcana][shot:insert window~]In the silver, for a single instant, she sees — she thinks she sees — a reflection that is not the lamp in her own window. Not her window at all. A different window. A different lamp. A different face.

[shot:insert window]She stands. She goes to the window. The rain is hitting the window hard. The cul-de-sac below is running with a thin sheet of water that is not, quite, flooding — the grid's quiet efficiency holding, as advertised — but that is, for the first time in Sam's memory, visible as a sheet, continuous, catching the overhead streetlight in a long rippling silver that extends across all three driveways opposite and down toward the storm drain at the bend.
She closes the notebook. She slides it between the mattress and the box spring.
She adds item 10: It is Wednesday. Diego has been missing for four days. I am going to find him. I do not need to find him today.
She looks at the list again. She adds item 9: Breathe.
[shot:closeup sam]She looks at the list. She crosses out item 3. She rewrites it: If Maya contacts me, answer in under five minutes. If Maya does not contact me, do not worry — she is working.
8. Write down everything dad says today. Every sentence. Even the boring ones. Patterns are in the boring.
7. Remember that whatever F.T. is, I am, right now, being watched by someone who wants to help. It is okay to let myself be watched.
6. If dad asks about last night's thunder, say I slept through it.
5. Eat lunch. Do not skip it.
4. If sedan shows up at Kwik Stop during my shift, do not acknowledge.
3. Do not contact Maya during her shift unless she contacts me first.
2. Do not go to the Gas & Go. Do not drive past the Gas & Go. Take the alternate route to Cosmic Comics if I go there.
1. Do not call dad during the day unless he calls first. If he calls first, answer on the third ring.
[shot:insert list]She is making a list. The list has a small header at the top in block capitals: WEDNESDAY LIST.

[mood:rain_interior]Sam has been awake since five-fifty-two. She is at her desk now, in her pajamas, with the lamp on against the grey of the storm. She has in front of her a notebook she bought at the Kwik Stop last night on her way home — one of the small cheap spiral-bound ones they stock for high-school kids, ninety-nine cents, lined pages, stapled on the short edge. She has not, until this summer, been a person who kept a notebook.

[mood:lunch][shot:establish]A customer at the counter asks for a refill on her coffee. Jesse pours it. Jesse smiles at her, the warm professional smile he has been using at the Pit Stop since he was fifteen. The customer smiles back. The customer does not know. The rain keeps coming.
Ben folds the bill. He puts it in the front pocket of his apron. The grill hisses. Jesse wipes his eyes with the back of his wrist.
Yeah, Jess. I've got it.
I need you to hold on to that bill for me.
Yeah.
Ben.
Yeah.
He's — he's fighting it.
Yeah, Jess.
He's trying.
[shot:closeup jesse]Jesse puts his hand on the counter. He does not cry. He breathes. He breathes for perhaps nine seconds.
Ben shows the bill to Jesse through the pass-through. Jesse reads it.

[shot:insert bill]Ben comes out of the office. He picks up the ten-dollar bill. On the back of it, in pencil, in handwriting neither Ben nor Jesse recognizes but that Ben will, the following morning, compare against the handwritten dedication page of a photograph album Jesse's mother will show him, the pencil has written: The red light lies. I am sorry. I will come back when I can.
