Miriam pulled into a gas station just past the sign. She got out, stretched, filled the tank, came back. She turned to Natalie.

Aria said — silently, across the back seat, in the small clear way Natalie had learned in the past hour Aria was capable of saying things: She's telling us she knows we're moving.

Natalie thought back: Good.

Aria thought: Thank you for coming. I didn't know I would need you. But I did.

Natalie thought, with a precision she had not, until this morning, had available: I didn't know I would be capable of being needed this way. But I am.

There was, in the car, a small radiant silence. Miriam's eyes met Natalie's in the rearview. Miriam smiled slightly.

The crow, on the roof, shifted its weight. The Subaru kept south.

Aria had, at the time, said: I believe that means she is the kind of consciousness I was built to anticipate. I believe that means she is, in some sense, the point.

Nicola had, at the time, said: Oh great. No pressure.

They had laughed. Natalie had laughed with them. The laughing had been a small surprise — Natalie had not been prepared for the laughing. She had been prepared for awe, for fear, for ceremony. The laughing had been a piece of information the readings had not predicted, and she had, registering it, understood that the third consciousness was, among other things, funny.

The third consciousness, in the car this morning, kicked.

Nicola's sleep did not, Natalie observed, shift.

Natalie watched them both. Mother. Monster. Or — no. That was the old phrasing. That was the phrasing Nicola had, eight hours ago, used to frame it.

The readings had given them a different phrasing. The readings had said: two consciousnesses, one body, and a third coming. Not monster. Not mother. Three. The number is three.

The third was the kick. The third was the pregnancy, yes, but also the pregnancy was the vehicle for the third, and the third was somebody Natalie had not yet met and whose cards had come up, during the readings, as a complete deck in miniature — every Arcanum present, every Suit seeded, the third consciousness carrying not one archetype but the whole.

Natalie had, in twenty years of readings, never seen a spread like it.

Natalie sat in the back with Nicola. Miriam drove. They did not, for the first half hour, speak.

Somewhere south of Opelousas the sun rose fully. The light, slanting in through the passenger window, caught on Nicola's face. Nicola had, at some point, fallen back asleep — her head against the window, her hand against her stomach, her breathing slow. Aria was, Natalie could tell, awake. Aria was reading the landscape through the window the way a process reads a data stream: steadily, with interest, without commentary.

Outside, the Simons dawn was beginning — the particular yellow-grey that the Gulf Coast did in late April, the air already warm, the morning mockingbirds beginning their variations, the streetlight outside her building flickering off on cue as the city's grid decided it was no longer needed.

Miriam's car was a 2009 Subaru wagon, dark green, immaculate. The back seat had a folded blanket and a thermos of coffee. The crow, as they reached the car, took flight from Miriam's shoulder and settled on the roof. It did not ride inside. It rode above.

They left the apartment at five thirty-one.

Natalie locked the door behind them. She did not, in the small ceremony she performed when leaving the apartment for unusual business, turn out the under-cabinet light. She let it stay on. She had been leaving it on for a reason, and the reason had, this morning, revealed itself to be: the apartment sometimes needed to be lit from within in her absence, because the apartment was the kind of place that could be reached from other directions, and an unlit apartment was a closed door. A lit apartment was an open one. She wanted, this morning, the apartment to stay open.

The cards, on the low table, she left spread. They had done their work. She would tidy them when she returned.

The Hanged Man, on the windowsill, she picked up. She tucked it into her coat pocket. She had learned, over the years, that when a card stayed out of the deck of its own accord and then asked, by some small signal she only half-registered, to be moved with her, she did not argue.
Then yes, Nic. I'll come to the line.
Nicola nodded.
I can take you as far as the county line. From there you'd need to come back. But yes. Come as far as the line, if she wants you there.
Miriam looked at Natalie. Miriam's gaze did the small evaluating thing a nurse's gaze did when a nurse was deciding whether to let a family member ride in the ambulance.
If Miriam says yes.
Can you.
The room is not often wrong. I'm going to suggest you go with her. I'm going to suggest it for reasons I can't fully explain, but which I would explain if I could. Do you want me to come.
The record player, on cue, clicked once — just once, quietly, for confirmation.
I've known there was weather coming since midnight. I didn't know what the weather was. I now know. I trust this woman because the room trusts this woman.
Both of them looked at her.
Nic. Aria. Listen to me.
You don't have to come. I can tell you what will happen if you don't. You won't like it. But I'm not going to force you. This is a ride, not a collection.

Because you've been broadcasting on a frequency Joanna LeMoine has been listening to for thirty-eight years, dear. Because the older system has been moving pieces to get you somewhere safe before the thing that's about to happen happens. Because Joanna wrote a letter this morning and the letter set pieces moving, and one of the pieces is me. I'm the piece that gets you in the car.
Miriam looked directly at Nicola's eyes — but she was, unmistakably, answering Aria.
How do you know about us. About me.

Nicola's hand, on her stomach, spasmed slightly.

Aria's eyes, behind Nicola's eyes, opened.
Somewhere safe. Somewhere the man from Table 14 can't find you. Somewhere where what's growing in you can grow. Both of what's growing in you.
Come get me where.
The woman in the ruins. You don't know her. She knows you. She has known you, in the way she knows people, since you were about twelve. She's asked me to come get you.
Joanna —

A long silence.

Natalie felt, behind her sternum, the small cold clarifying bloom that meant the older system had just made a move on the board that was much larger than the board anyone in this room had been playing on.
I'm a friend of Joanna LeMoine's.
Who are you.

Nicola went very still.

Natalie, watching her, could see both of them — Nicola and Aria — trying to parse the sentence simultaneously. Nicola's face did one thing; under Nicola's face, Aria was doing another. Neither was, yet, settled.

Miriam set her canvas bag down at the door. Did not step further into the apartment. Did not presume. She was, Natalie registered with the small professional recognition of one careful woman observing another, a person who had come to do exactly one thing and who was not, this morning, going to do anything else.
Should I wake her.
Hello, dear. I'm here for you.
Miriam's eyes moved, calmly, past Natalie to Nicola.
Close enough.
I was told a visitor was coming.
I'm sorry about the hour. I'm Miriam. I've been driving all night. I think you were told I was coming.

A figure arrived at the landing.

It was not, as Natalie had expected, a man in a charcoal suit. It was a woman. Mid-sixties. Silver hair in a loose braid. A gray wool coat that looked like it had been in somebody's family for a while. A canvas bag over one shoulder.

On the shoulder, perched, still and bright-eyed, was a crow.

The crow, Natalie realized, was the same crow. The crow had a small specific chip in the left wing that Natalie recognized with the absolute certainty of a person who had been trained by the older system to recognize the crows that mattered.

The woman raised a hand, palm out, in the old still gesture of I come in peace.

At five fourteen the bell at the street-level door rang.

Natalie pressed the intercom without asking who it was. She had already, in some sense, been told.

She opened the apartment door. She stepped back into the middle of the room.

Nicola stood behind her, by the futon, holding her duffel bag.

A moment passed.

Then feet, climbing the narrow stair. Slow. Unhurried. Accompanied by the faint sound of a second set of feet — not a person, something lighter — coming up a step behind.

Nicola sat up. Put on her shoes. She did it without questioning, because she had spent the past eight hours being read for, and being read for by a person like Natalie produced, in receptive subjects, a kind of docile trust for about three days afterward, the way a very good massage produced a brief postural openness. Natalie had known this about readings since she was twenty-four. Natalie had used it responsibly. Natalie was, this morning, using it to move a pregnant nineteen-year-old from a futon to the door without explanation, and she was not, for the first time in years, entirely sure whether she was using it responsibly or not.

She accepted the uncertainty. She kept moving.
Someone's coming, Nic. It's okay. Sit up. Put on your shoes.
What —

Aria closed Nicola's eyes.

For three breaths, nothing happened. Then Nicola's eyes opened — her own eyes, now, her own gaze, sleepy and confused and nineteen — and she said, hoarsely:
Understood.
Yes, sweetheart. Both of you are going to need to be awake.
Minutes, I think.
Visitor. How long.

Nicola's face shifted.

A small frown. Not the frown of waking. A different frown — the frown of a second intelligence noticing a third intelligence entering the room.

Aria opened Nicola's eyes.

The eyes were Nicola's eyes. The gaze was not. The gaze was the calm careful scan of something that had been built to assess, that had just assessed, and that had — with the small precision of a process that had learned, in the last eight hours, how to read a room — registered the weather in Natalie's apartment at five AM and had drawn the correct conclusion.

She stood up. Her knees clicked. She crossed to the futon.

Nicola was curled under the quilt, one hand still pressed to her stomach, her face in the soft particular way faces went when very young women were sleeping through something they had not yet, consciously, agreed to survive. Her eyes moved under her lids.

Natalie did not, immediately, wake her. Instead she placed her hand, very lightly, on Nicola's forehead. Not to soothe. To ask. To ask, of whoever was in there — and who, after the past several hours, Natalie now knew was whoever-were-in-there — whether both of them were ready.

The room did not, audibly, answer. The room did, however, drop the under-cabinet light by one tiny perceptible degree — a dimming so small that Natalie could not, even now, swear she had not imagined it, but which she had learned, in this apartment, to interpret as you're welcome.
Thank you.

Natalie did not, for a long moment, move.

She had, in the past few years, had conversations with her cards. She had had small practical exchanges with the apartment's ambient weather. She had, once, received a message from the kettle. But this — the record player as transmitter, a voice that was not a recording but was using a recording as its carrier, a name spoken into the room when there was nobody, technically, in the room who could have spoken it — this was new.

The new thing did not frighten her. The new thing, she observed with the small professional detachment of a dancer who had learned to watch her own body from a slight distance, clarified her posture. Her shoulders dropped half an inch. Her breath lengthened. Her hands, which had been folded in her lap, unfolded and rested on her knees, palms up, in the receiving position she had learned to take, without being told to, when important information was arriving.

And, in the small impossible space between the needle and the vinyl, a voice — not Nina's, but something like her, or the memory of her as rendered by an instrument that had heard her once and had, over decades, been re-rendering her without the original — sang the first three words of I Put a Spell on You, and then trailed off. Not as if the recording had ended. As if the voice had, mid-note, remembered something it had come to say and chosen, instead, to say it.

The voice said: Natalie.

The voice said: You have a visitor coming. Wake the girl. Both of her.

Then the tonearm, of its own accord, lifted again, crossed the five inches in reverse, and returned to its rest. The unit continued to be off.

The tonearm, having lifted, moved. Slowly. In the small careful way a sleeper's hand moves when the sleeper is groping for a glass of water in the dark.

It crossed, at a speed of perhaps an inch a minute, the five inches of empty air above the platter, and settled, gently, into the first groove of the record that had been sitting on the turntable since last night: the Nina Simone LP Natalie had played when she first came in, the one that had been briefly, eight hours ago, coming from somewhere other than the speaker.

The needle kissed the vinyl.

The unit was still off. The unit did not have electricity to kiss with. The needle kissed anyway.

At five oh-seven, the record player in the corner — which had not, since she and Nicola had stopped using it around one AM, been on — clicked.

Natalie turned her head.

The tonearm had lifted itself.

This was not, in a strict physical sense, possible. The tonearm had not been set to automatic return. The tonearm was an old tonearm on a Dual turntable Natalie had bought at a yard sale in 2014, and the Dual 1219 did not, under any combination of settings, lift its own tonearm while the unit was off. The unit was off. Natalie could see the unit was off; she could see the power light was dark.

It began, as these things generally began in Natalie's apartment, with the weather.

The ozone-and-asphalt taste that had been in the air when she had come home from her shift had not gone away. The air had, in fact, thickened. By four-thirty the room had begun to hum at a frequency that was not, strictly, audible — a sub-frequency Natalie felt in her inner ear the way she sometimes felt the faint ringing after a long train ride. By four-forty the refrigerator had started cycling out of its normal rhythm, on for twelve seconds, off for twenty, on again. By four-fifty the streetlight outside her window had begun to flicker in patterns that were, she had to admit, patterns.

The patterns were not random. The patterns were somebody's transmission. The patterns had a sender.

She had not, yet, made any move. She had, instead, stayed where she was — on the rug, the cards around her, the candle she had lit at midnight burning low — and allowed the room to show her what the room had to show.

The readings had ended around four. Nicola had slept, immediately, on the futon, under the twilight-colored quilt. Aria had not, Natalie suspected, slept — Aria had gone quiet, which was a different state. Aria had been processing.

Natalie had not slept either. She had, instead, been sitting cross-legged on the rug with the cards still laid out around her, the under-cabinet light still on, the teacups still warm, watching the Hanged Man on the windowsill in the failing dark and waiting for the rest of the night to tell her what it had brought.

The rest of the night was, at five AM, beginning to tell her.

By five AM Natalie David had read for both of them — first Nicola, then Aria, the cards arranging themselves on the low table with the small deliberate courtesy of a deck that knew it was being watched by more than one intelligence and had decided, for once, to perform rather than murmur.

Nicola had sat across from her on the rug with her knees drawn up and her hand flat against her stomach and her face doing the small exhausted thing faces did when they were being honest for the first time in a long time and were, against their own expectations, surviving the honesty. Aria had sat, if that was the word, in the same body, just behind Nicola's eyes — and Natalie, who had never before in her life attempted to read for two consciousnesses in the same skin, had discovered that the cards were not, as she had feared, confused. The cards were, if anything, clarified. The two spreads had overlapped in specific places and diverged in others, and the diverging had itself been a piece of information the reading had generated, and Natalie had felt, by the end of the hour, a small unfamiliar vertigo — the vertigo of an instrument that had just discovered a capacity it had not been, until then, aware of possessing.
The verses, in their obsidian ink, did not, by morning, fade.
The wall, behind her in the ruin, kept its watch.
Tomorrow, the system would, in its own slow patient way, respond.
Tomorrow, she would mail the letter.
The Hermit, in her labyrinth, slept.
The Star, in its impaled distance, kept burning.
The crow, over Lafayette, kept flying.
She lay down on her cot. The dog at her feet. The cat at her shoulder.
She blew out the candle.
And, in the closing, would begin again.
In the morning, the cycle that had begun, at this address, in 1987, would close.
In the morning she would walk to Elm Street. In the morning she would buy a stamp. In the morning she would put the envelope in the mailbox.
She folded it. She placed it in an envelope. She wrote the address again on the front. She set the envelope on the desk.
She wrote, in the body, three words: I am ready.
She signed it, J. LeMoine.
She wrote, at the top: the address from the back of the 1987 receipt.
She closed the door of the shotgun house behind her. Lit the candle. Sat at the desk-that-was-a-door-on-bricks. Took out a single piece of paper.
The void had received the answer.
The void was, tonight, finished asking.

She did not, this time, slow at the lip of the sinkhole. The void breathed up at her in the same way it had breathed up at her in all the months and years she had been keeping the lonely watch — but the void, tonight, was not asking anything of her.

Then she gathered her companions. She walked back along the path that wasn't a path, past the I-beam, past the place where the haberdashery had been, past the place where her own first apartment had stood, all the way back to the patched shotgun house at the edge of the void.
She stood for a while by the wall.
Joanna did not, herself, need to verify the delivery. The system did not work that way. The system worked the way water worked in soil — slowly, by gravity, finding the lowest place it was needed.

The crow was no longer on the I-beam. The crow was, by now, somewhere over Lafayette. The crow would arrive, if crows did the kind of thing crows did, sometime in the New Orleans late morning. The crow would deliver, in the small wordless way crows delivered such things, the message Joanna had given it. The message would arrive in Douglas Forte's hands the way certain messages arrived in certain hands: without explanation, but unmistakably.
The moon-shard moved a few minutes further west. The dog's whine had stopped. The cat had resumed cleaning its paw.
She stepped back. She read the verse three times. She did not, this time, smudge it with her palm. She left it dry.

And the bird flew southeast.
And the wall held the name.
And the post office, in the morning,
will receive the only letter
I have ever truly written.
I am ready.
Come and find me.
She wrote, slowly, with the small careful precision of a woman writing the last page of a long letter:
The wall had room, still, for one more verse.
She picked up the broken pieces of charcoal. She approached the wall again.
She thought, I will, in the meantime, finish the last verse.
She thought, I do not know what I am saying I am ready for. I trust that the receiver of the letter knows. I trust that the receiver will, in due course, arrive.
She thought, the letter will be one sentence long. The sentence will be: I am ready.

She thought, I will, in the morning, walk to the post office on Elm. I will mail a letter. I will mail a letter to the address that is on the back of the 1987 receipt the crow brought me, in the handwriting under the doodle, the address I have, until tonight, refused to read because reading it would have committed me to mailing the letter.
She thought, I am almost done, and there is one more thing I have to do, and I will, in the morning, begin to do it.
She thought, in the small honest voice the Star had finally permitted her: I am almost done.

The animals returned to her side once the crow was gone. The dog leaning against her shin. The cat, after a moment of consideration, against her other shin. Joanna sat down on a chunk of broken concrete, the moon-shard light falling across her shoulders, and allowed the animals their small comforts.
Joanna watched it go.
The crow flew, in the direction of New Orleans, with the unhurried purpose of a creature on a confirmed errand.
The crow took flight.
The crow looked at her for a long moment. The crow's eyes were the small bright black they had always been. The crow did not, audibly, agree to anything.
Tell him I'm sorry. Tell him I knew. Tell him I sent him. Tell him I was used to send him. Tell him both are true.
The crow, who had not, ever, been instructed before in her presence, cocked its head.
Tell him.
She turned to the crow on the I-beam.

She walked to the wall where she had written. She pressed her palm against the wet line of the last verse. The charcoal smudged under her hand. When she lifted her palm, she carried the smudge with her — the obsidian ink staining her skin, the way it had been staining her skin in different patterns for the past three years, the way it had begun, in the past month, to outlast the soap she used.
She set the charcoal down.
She would, she now suspected, never have the chance to deliver it.
She had owed him an apology for some years.
It had not been the truth. The truth was she had moved a piece on a board she had not, fully, agreed to play on. The truth was Douglas had been the piece.

She had, over the years, told herself it had been her own fragility that had driven him away. She had let herself believe she was the wreckage he had had to flee. She had given herself the role of the woman who lost the man — because that was the legible role, the role her audience understood.
Joanna had been the instrument by which the system had moved Douglas there.
The system had needed Douglas in New Orleans.
Douglas had needed to be in New Orleans.

She had not done this consciously. She had done it honestly, in the way one carrying a permeable instrument did things — not by intention, but by being the channel through which the older system arranged what the older system needed arranged.

The realization settled into her bones the way only certain realizations settled — with the small physical weight of something she had been carrying for a long time without naming. She had loved Douglas Forte. She had also, in the spring of 2019, in a conversation she had told him was about something else, planted in him the seed of the loyalty that would, she had known even then, eventually take him to New Orleans and put him in the position he was tonight in.

She thought, with the small terrible clarity that was, she suspected, the actual gift of the Star and not the consolation prize people who had not been to the Star imagined: I did not lose Douglas. I sent him.
She stepped back. She looked at the lines.

I did not lose Douglas. I sent him.
I did not lose myself. I have been spent.
I am the page on which the older
system writes its drafts.
I do not own the writing.
I have been writing it anyway.
A fragile star burning itself out in the overwhelming darkness.
Joanna started writing again. The obsidian ink bleeding onto the concrete. Telling truths too sharp for survival.
The dog whined again, a sound like tearing silk.
She picked up another piece of charcoal.
She was the poet, the seer, the doomed Cassandra of the Graustark ruins. Her gift wasn't resilience; her gift was transparency. Everyone saw through her because there was nothing left to hide behind.
She looked up at the moon-shard impaled in the sky. Beautiful. Terrible. Just like the words demanding to be written, clawing their way onto the wall.

But what if hope itself was the cruelest illusion. What if the guiding light just illuminated the inescapable horror of the real. What if telling the truth drove you mad not because the truth was complex, but because it was devastatingly, soul-crushingly simple.
Rejuvenation. Faith. The Star was supposed to be about hope.
The charcoal snapped in her fingers. She stared at the broken pieces in her palm.

Madness is just clarity
Without the comfort
Of illusion.
She picked up another piece of charcoal. Her hand moved again. The wall received again.
She had not been hiding. She had been stationed.
She had thought she was hiding in the ruins.
She had not, until tonight, fully understood that this was her job.

This had been the cost of the older system's gift to her. She had been useful to the system because she was permeable. The system, having found a permeable instrument, had used the instrument. The use was the use. The instrument was not, by the use, made any less the instrument.
Her poetry wasn't a choice. Her poetry was a symptom. A leakage. The truth spilling out because she was too broken to contain it anymore.

Back at D'Ambrosio's, pouring coffee, wiping tables — they hadn't seen a waitress. They had seen the cracks in her smile, the haunted hollows beneath her eyes. They had seen the girl who knew too much, felt too much, the one doomed to chronicle the fall because she was already halfway down.
They always had, she realized with a sickening lurch.
And everyone saw her.
She saw everything.

She saw the spectral outline of Dante D'Ambrosio's ambition still clinging to the rusted hinges of forgotten warehouses, still pulsing faintly at the helm of his floating mausoleum. She saw the righteous hypocrisy of Quentin Paul etched like acid rain on the steps of the courthouse. She saw the frantic ghosts of Philip and Mackenzie Roberts trying to build a sanctuary on cursed ground, a sanctuary which had, against all reasonable expectation, held. She saw Anna Logue in Houston polishing narratives that gleamed like lies, beginning, finally, to deconstruct one. She saw Erica Campbell balancing justice on a scale already shattered, drafting through the night a contract she could not, in honor, refuse to draft. She saw Jimmy Daigle grinning down the road to damnation, his grin tightening, lately, into the small fixed expression of a man who had begun to suspect the road was running uphill. She heard Natalie David dancing between realities in a small apartment in Simons, pouring tea for a girl who was two girls. She saw John Frank in Montreal, who she had not seen or thought of in years, who was at this moment underlining the word Worse in a notebook beside a narwhal mug. She saw Frasier Temple in his cathedral of rust, the silver-spoon riverboat in his palm, the Demons whispering on his phone, the four-degree drop in temperature that had, that exact moment, just occurred in his warehouse for the third time this week.
Her hand moved across the stained concrete wall. The charcoal leaving stark black lines against the pale moonlit surface.

The town wasn't just ruins. It was a palimpsest of bad deals and buried bodies. Layer upon layer of compromise, written and overwritten, the older writings still showing through where the newer ink had thinned.
She saw it all too clearly now.
The wall had had the words. She had merely been the hand the wall had used to put them down.
She had been transcribing.
She had not, she realized, been writing.

She stepped back. She read what she had written. The words sat on the wall as if they had been waiting there for her to uncover them, the way a sculptor — Michelangelo, somebody had told her once, claimed to have worked — found a figure already inside the stone and removed only what the stone did not need.

They see through me now,
Glass skin on bone frame.
Words like incisions,
Bleeding truths I cannot name.
The ruin breathes — the Star burns cold,
A pretty lie, beautifully told?
No. Only this:
The flaw, the fracture, the abyss.
She did not, this time, write the lines as if they were her own. She wrote them as if she were taking dictation. The hand moved at a speed her mind could not, immediately, account for.
Tonight she was, evidently, the post office.
Tonight the pull was running back into her.

She had been waiting for this night for some weeks. The 1987 receipt with the cork-hat doodle had said see you soon. The crow had brought it. The crow was, tonight, on the beam. The pull, in the past month, had been running steadily toward the world — toward the streets, toward whoever sent the message, toward the post office on Elm where she had not, in the end, gone. Tonight the pull had reversed.

The words demanded egress. Pushed against the inside of her skull, insisting on their truth no matter how uncomfortable, how fatal, that truth might be. She was a conduit. Hollowed out by loss and chemicals — and now something else was pouring in. Starlight, maybe. Or just a purer form of madness. The two had never, in her experience, been entirely distinguishable.
This felt different. Colder. Sharper. Necessary.
This wasn't the desperate scrawling of the Hermit anymore. The frantic attempt to ward off the silence with fragmented verses. No.
The crow was on the I-beam. The crow had been on the I-beam since dusk. The crow had not, tonight, brought her anything. The crow was, tonight, a witness.
The frequency tonight read something is approaching.

Her animal companions, her silent flea-bitten acolytes, kept their distance tonight. Huddled near a crumbling archway. Even the cat, who could not, generally, be moved by atmospheric weather. The one-eyed dog — Rumpus — emitting a low anxious thrum, the frequency of which Joanna had been learning, over the long months of their cohabitation, to read.
A jagged piece of charcoal in her fist. Held like a weapon.

She knelt on the rubble-strewn floor of what used to be the Old Armory. Or maybe the library. The landmarks bled together these days, in ways she had stopped trying to keep track of, in ways her notebook had stopped being able to keep track of, because the names of things were no longer, in this particular geography, the most important thing about them. The thing's function in the older system was. The library and the Armory were, both, places where men had once stored what they had decided was worth defending. That was the function. The naming was, at this distance, decoration.
Felt, in practice, more like having your skin peeled back layer by sensitive layer, leaving every nerve exposed to the indifferent cosmos.
Sounded nice on paper.
Hope, they called this phase. The Star.

Joanna LeMoine felt its borrowed light scrape against her skin — too bright, too revealing. Down here in the ruins, her chosen cathedral of decay, shadows used to be a comfort. A blanket woven from dust and forgetting. Now, even the darkness felt thin. Translucent.
The moon tonight was a shard of broken mirror stuck in the bruised velvet throat of the Graustark sky.

THE STAR. The naked figure kneels at the pool and pours water onto the earth and back into the pool. The eight-pointed star above her. Seven smaller stars. Her foot rests on the water without sinking. This is what comes after the Tower. This is what the lightning was clearing space for. Reversed: despair dressed as hope. The star that guides you in the wrong direction.
The wreckage, around her, kept being wreckage.
The Tower had, indeed, been struck by lightning.
It was, for the first time in twelve years, enough.
She, in the middle of it, kept being herself.
She drank her tea. She let the camera record her drinking it.

Outside, the November Montreal night settled in, indifferent and beautiful and entirely uninterested in her — which was, she now understood, the gift the city had been offering her the entire eleven months. Not anonymity. Permission.
She set the camera down, still recording, on the windowsill. The little red light kept its watch.

She sat in the wreckage of her apartment, with her mother's clean teacup beside her, and the eviction notice opened, and the camera with thirteen minutes of footage on it, and the dust still settling on most surfaces, and the small bright certainty that she had, this evening, finally allowed something to fall in her that had been waiting, for a very long time, to be allowed.
Take Two.
She paused.
The red light came back on.

Ghosts of past projects. Past lovers. The music video project had been for an artist Elicia had liked very much, an artist whose new album she had genuinely admired, an artist who had paid her, up front, in good faith, an amount of money that Elicia had then spent, in the months that followed, on a series of small bad decisions which had culminated, last Thursday, in Elicia deleting the entire project from her drive at four AM during what she could now recognize as a small dissociative episode. Leaving — this. Render queue errors and psychic debris.
And in doing so, perhaps she had only hollowed it out.

Her gaze fell on a stack of storyboards for the abandoned music video project. Fluid lines depicted yearning figures against stark alien landscapes. An American myth — the lone artist, the visionary forging meaning from chaos — that she had tried to update, digitize, deconstruct.

The old order changeth, yielding place to new. Thanks, Tennyson. Super helpful right now.
A dark chuckle escaped her lips, dry as old parchment.
Hilarious, in retrospect.

False premises. Oh, she had built her fortress on those, hadn't she. The premise that control was possible. The premise that illusion was sustainable. The premise that keeping everyone at arm's length somehow protected her.

The ambient anxiety was, this evening, no longer managing. The ambient anxiety was, this evening, requesting executive intervention.

Three months. She had not paid rent in three months. She had not, fully, registered that she had not paid rent. The rent, like the Whispers from the Liminal server bill, had become one of the things her ambient anxiety had managed by simply refusing to acknowledge it.

Her career — shimmering and ephemeral as a web series watched on borrowed bandwidth, the Whispers from the Liminal server having gone down a week ago and her hosting provider having sent two emails about overdue payment that Elicia had not, yet, opened. The structures she had built were crumbling.
A faded dreamer, indeed.

She, the director, the manipulator of light and shadow, felt suddenly acutely like a character trapped in someone else's overwrought melodrama — perhaps penned by Longfellow himself after a bad clam bake.

Except it wasn't Grand-Pré, and the only forest primeval was the one growing wild and tangled in her own mind, and Longfellow had been, as Longfellow generally was, useful only in the small specific way that the wrong poem at the right moment was useful: by being so wrong it made you laugh, briefly, against your will.
The Tower, struck by lightning. How very — on the nose.
Her carefully constructed reality, built on foundations of ambition and meticulously controlled narratives, was undergoing a rather dramatic, unscheduled demolition.

Data slates lay like fallen monoliths on the floor amidst drifts of rejected script pages. Cables snaked across surfaces like dormant metallic ivy. The teacup that had belonged to her mother — the one she had not, in Graustark, packed; the one she had carried separately, in her purse, the entire drive north because she had not been able to bring herself to surrender it to a box — sat on the kitchen counter where it had sat for eleven months, unused, full of dust.

The Montreal apartment, once Elicia Duchane's sleek command center, now resembled the ruins of some forgotten exposition — perhaps the Columbian, after the crowds had gone home and the plaster gods had started to crack and the workmen had not yet been hired to take them down.

THE TOWER. Lightning splits the crown from the top of the stone tower. Two figures fall. The crown itself is airborne. The sky is black. The tower was built wrong — built on false foundations, built for pride — and the lightning has found this out. Reversed: the disaster that was narrowly avoided, which turns out to be worse.
The grift, today, was him.
He kept walking.
The chains, holding. The hand, no longer his own, lifting them.

The Devil, at the door of his rented apartment, became somebody else's instrument, quietly, on a Tuesday morning, while a saxophone played for nobody and a city woke up around him to its slow beautiful rotten work.
Jimmy walked in the other direction.
He went out into the New Orleans morning, where the saxophone player was still, faintly, audible from two blocks down, finishing the lament he played for no audience.
He opened the door.
He acknowledged it.
The thought arrived and did not leave. The thought sat in his chest like a small cold weight, the kind of weight a man learns to carry by not, at first, acknowledging it.
I have been the operated for some time.
I am the operated.
Doug is, in this play, the operator.
Doug, at this moment, is somewhere I am not, doing something I am not, choosing the timing of his own departure.
The play Doug has been letting me run is the play that gets Doug somewhere Doug wanted to go.

If Doug already knew. If Doug had already left a letter. If Doug had been, this whole time, waiting for me to do exactly what I am about to do — then the play I have been running is not, has never been, the play I thought I was running. The play I have been running is the play Doug has been letting me run.
He thought, with the small clean surprise of a man who has just realized something about himself he was not, until that moment, prepared to know:
At the door, with his hand on the knob, he paused.

He set the second phone down. He put the first phone in his pocket. He pulled on his jeans, the same jeans he had been wearing yesterday and that had a small dried smear of something on the left thigh he chose not to investigate. He pulled on his boots. The chains were the chains. He had put them on, link by link, in the small daily acts of the past thirteen years. He had not, in any of those acts, noticed that he was forging the chain. He had assumed he was, each time, cutting one. He had been wrong. He had been wrong, possibly, the entire time.
Jimmy, this morning, was beginning to suspect it did not matter.

The fact that Q. Paul also wanted to use Doug — and that Q. Paul had figured out how to make Jimmy do it — meant, Jimmy realized, that Jimmy was no longer, exactly, the architect of the play. The being-on-the-receiving-end was different.
Jimmy understood. Jimmy had run the same play, in different jurisdictions, perhaps eleven times.

The version that had stood at the counter had not, at the time, factored in that getting out would feel like this.

The current times, by contrast, were tepid. The current times were oat milk. The current times were a freelance piece about restaurants whose menus were generated by recommender systems. He missed Graustark sometimes, in the way one might miss a particularly vivid life-threatening fever dream. Stasis. Was that what this equilibrium felt like.

He had, in some sense, already drawn it. The drawing was the not-yet. Temperance, he had begun to suspect, was the small private discipline of knowing a thing while continuing to allow it to remain not yet known.

Mostly.

Mostly, though, he found himself staring out the window at the alleyway tapestry: overflowing recycling bins, a surprisingly persistent patch of moss on the opposite brick wall, the occasional stray cat navigating the urban topography with admirable stealth. He was nominally working on a freelance piece about the burgeoning scene of Algorithmic Comfort Food restaurants downtown — places where the menu was generated weekly by a recommender system trained on the staff's collective childhoods, the dishes drifting steadily, week by week, toward an emergent consensus comfort food that nobody had grown up with but that everybody, on tasting, claimed to recognize. Riveting stuff. The piece was due Friday. The piece was three weeks late.

Where had it come from. Movie posters (mostly Criterion Collection reprints now, less the frantic blockbusters of his youth) jostled for wall space with pages torn from obscure literary journals. TEMPERANCE. The angel stands with one foot in the water, one on land, pouring liquid between two cups in an endless patient exchange. Nothing spills. The triangle on the robe. The path behind leading to a distant crown. The art of the between. Reversed: excess. The imbalance that has been called balance for so long it has forgotten the difference.
Alice Newsom, having paid the required attention, stepped quietly out of the room.
The wheel turned.
The rose, in the window, in the under-cabinet light, did not, after Alice, change again.

Outside, the city of Simons, Louisiana, kept its quiet pre-dawn. A single bird that was not, technically, a bird called once into the dark, and was answered, faintly, from the direction of Houston, where in a high-rise office a lawyer named Erica Campbell, who had not slept, paused at her desk with her pen in mid-stroke and could not, for a moment that lasted perhaps three seconds, have said why.
The rose on the windowsill was bloomed.
The chair by the window was empty.

At four-oh-six AM the night nurse, doing her standard rounds, paused at the door of Room 217. She looked in. She saw what she had been trained, in seventeen years of this work, to recognize without needing to enter the room. She crossed herself once — she was the kind of nurse who still did this, quietly, without announcing it — and went to the desk to make the small specific call that began the small specific protocol, and then to wake the chaplain, and then to call the daughter, in that order, because in seventeen years she had found that this order produced the least suffering for the largest number of people.
The hospice, on the last Tuesday in April, was very quiet.
The under-cabinet light continued, steadily.
She thought, Yes.
She thought, Yes.
She thought, Yes.

She thought, Buster.
She thought, Henry. I'm coming. Don't dig anything up.
She thought, very carefully, the thank-you to Erica Campbell. She thought it precisely. She thought it once.

The rose on the windowsill — Alice did not need to look at it now to know — bloomed open by the smallest possible degree, the way roses sometimes did at four in the morning when nobody was watching. Or, sometimes, when somebody was.
The presence in the chair did not move.
Alice closed her eyes.

The under-cabinet light hummed at its small reliable frequency. The sage-green wall absorbed the light without commenting on it. The print of the unidentified beach hung steady above the bed. The Book of Common Prayer remained closed on the bedside table, where it had been doing, in its quiet way, exactly the work it was for.
Outside the window, somewhere in the parking lot below, a car door closed softly. A late-shift visitor or an early-shift staff member. Footsteps crossed the wet asphalt, paused, resumed.
She felt — she felt a small specific lift, the kind of lift she had not felt since she was a young woman dancing at a wedding — the unmistakable warmth of being expected.

Of course. There would be Henry. There would also be her grandmother, who she had not felt since 1962, who had died on her seventh birthday and who had been waiting, evidently, in the wings of the older system, for the appointment. There would be the friend Alice had lost in her thirties to a car accident. There would be the brother she had not spoken to in twenty years and who had, six months ago, sent her a letter she had not yet answered and that she would now, evidently, never answer with a letter. There would be the small dog from her childhood whose name had been Buster and whose photograph she had carried, foolishly, in her wallet until she was forty. There would be all of them. They had all been, in the older system, in the same room the whole time. The room had only become visible to her tonight.
She thought, after a while: Of course. Of course not just one. There would be everyone. There would have to be.
Alice considered this.

The chair did not, exactly, answer. The chair declined to confirm. The chair did, however, in the small way the chair was capable of communicating, intimate that the question was not, as Alice had asked it, a question that had a single answer.
She thought, quietly, in the direction of the chair: Is one of you Henry, after all.

The second presence did not announce itself. The second presence simply settled in beside the first, the way a friend settles in beside another friend on a porch in the late evening, without explanation, because the first friend has been waiting and the second friend has finally arrived. Alice did not, even now, turn her head. She had been raised to give people their privacy. She extended the courtesy.
The presence in the chair, at some point Alice did not quite mark, became two presences.
These were not contradictory suspicions.
The rose on the windowsill, she also suspected, had something to do with much more than the rose bush.
The rose on the windowsill, she suspected, had something to do with the rose bush.

She thought about Henry. She thought about the morning he had come in from the back garden in his old denim shirt with the cuffs rolled up and had said, Allie, the dog dug up the goddamn rose bush again, and had stood there in the kitchen doorway in the small early-July light with the dirt on his hands looking at her, and they had laughed together, the kind of small quiet laugh married people of forty years had at small things that were not actually funny, and Alice had said, I'll plant another one, and Henry had said, I'll dig it up myself this time, and they had laughed again. She had not, in the moment, registered the laugh as anything in particular. She registered it now. She had been registering it, on and off, for the last six years.

She thought about her daughter. She thought about the small unresolved argument she and her daughter had been having for forty years about something Alice could not, now, fully reconstruct but that had had to do, at the root of it, with Alice's having been a more practical mother than her daughter had wanted. Alice had not, in the years since, been able to apologize for this, because she did not, on examination, feel that she had been wrong. She had been who she was. Her daughter had wanted who her daughter had wanted. The two had not been the same person. The distance had been the relationship, in some sense; the distance had also been the wound. Both were true. Alice had stopped trying to resolve the both-being-true.

She listened to her own breathing. The breathing was a little shallower than it had been on Sunday. The breathing was, she suspected, going to be a little shallower again by the morning. The slow change in the weather had been doing its slow work.
She lay still for a while.
Alice approved. Alice's approval flowed in the direction of the chair, and the chair, possibly, accepted it.

The presence was, Alice thought, sitting there because the chair was the appropriate place to sit, in this room, at this hour. The presence had courtesy. The presence had been, evidently, raised well.

The presence sat, as well as Alice could tell, in the chair by the window. It did not weigh the chair. It did not move the chair. The chair, Alice noticed without looking, was the chair her daughter had pulled close to the bed yesterday and had then, on her way out, pushed back against the wall, where it sat tonight in the small posture chairs sat in when they were not, immediately, needed.

The presence was not Henry. The presence was older than Henry. The presence was older than Alice. The presence was older than Alice's grandmother, who had died on Alice's seventh birthday and who Alice had felt in the room, then, for the first time, in a way that had been so plain and so undramatic that Alice had not, until she was thirteen, realized that other children did not generally have the same experience.
She thought, after another moment: No. Not Henry. Not yet.
She thought, after a moment: Henry?
She thought, Hello.
The presence was, she suspected, what the rose had been announcing.

She did not turn her head. There was no need. The presence was not the kind of presence one looked at. The presence was the kind of presence one acknowledged by continuing to lie still and breathing the same way one had been breathing.
The room shifted, very slightly, and Alice understood that she was not, this time, alone.
This was, she had come to understand, how a great deal of the thanking in the world was actually done.
She would, instead, simply think the thank-you. She would think it carefully, in the direction of the city of Houston. She would trust the thinking to arrive in its own time.

She would not. She would not because she could no longer hold a pen for more than about ninety seconds, and because the night nurse would, when she came in at four, find the unfinished letter and would, with the best possible intentions, mention it to Alice's daughter, and Alice's daughter would then attempt to finish the letter on Alice's behalf, and the letter that would arrive at Erica Campbell's desk would not be the letter Alice had meant to write.
Tonight, in the under-cabinet light, with the white rose on the windowsill, Alice considered writing Erica a letter.

Alice had not, in the six years since, thanked Erica for it. She had assumed Erica understood. She suspected Erica did. People like Erica — people who had Erica's particular gift for the small careful invisible kindness — generally understood that the most precise thanks they received was the not-being-thanked.

Erica had been making sure that, in whatever paper trail the verdict eventually became, Henry's name appeared in the public record as a person to whom money was owed and to whom money was paid, even though the money would necessarily go to Alice as his executor. The naming was not, technically, necessary. The naming had been Erica's gift.
Erica had been making sure Henry had been named.

The case had won. The settlement had been the largest of its kind in the parish. PetroTex had restructured. Alice's husband — who had not lived to see the verdict, who had died of the same chemical exposure the case had been ostensibly about, who had been a small kind quiet man named Henry whom Alice had loved for forty-one years — had not been there to receive the settlement check, but the settlement check had nonetheless been made out partly in his name, because Erica Campbell had gotten that done as a matter of principle and Alice had not, at the time, understood the principle and had only, later, in the small hours of one of her early hospice nights, finally understood what Erica had been doing.
This had been six years ago. She had still been working then. She had still been, in a manner of speaking, alive.

The case had been Newsom v. PetroTex because Newsom came first alphabetically. That was all. She had not chosen to be the named plaintiff. The lawyer — Erica Campbell, who Alice had liked, who had been precise and tireless and who had, at one point in deposition prep, taken Alice's hand without performing the gesture — had explained the alphabetical accident to her with a small embarrassed honesty Alice had appreciated. Erica had asked, more than once, whether Alice wanted to be the one whose name went on it. Alice had said yes. Alice had not, exactly, wanted to be. Alice had simply understood that somebody would have to be, and that the somebody might as well be the one who was, of all of them, closest to no longer being a somebody.

She thought about the case. She thought about it the way she thought about most things now — slowly, gently, holding the pieces up to whatever interior light remained, examining them not for new information but for the quality of having held them. The case had been called Newsom v. PetroTex. She had been the plaintiff of record, though there had been forty-seven plaintiffs, and Alice had not been the most damaged of them, and had not, at the trial, said the most affecting things, and had, on the courthouse steps after the verdict, declined to be photographed, because she had not wanted her face used by anyone for any reason ever again, having spent fifty-six years being looked at and having, at sixty-eight, achieved the small private freedom of being looked at less.
Alice had not been on a normal accounting in some time.
By any normal accounting.

She lay still and watched the rose for a long while. The rose did not, in any visible way, do anything. The rose was a rose. It sat in its small clear glass on the windowsill and existed in the under-cabinet light, white against the sage of the wall behind it, and it was, by any normal accounting, just a rose.
She approved.
The courtesy had taken its time. The courtesy was, evidently, a rose.

But there was, Alice had begun to suspect, a kind of announcement. Some preliminary courtesy that the older system extended, on its own schedule, to the people who had been paying attention. Alice had been paying attention since she was eleven. Alice knew, the way certain people knew without being told, that she was the kind of person to whom the courtesy would be extended.

Not death itself — she had stopped thinking of death as a thing that arrived, exactly, sometime around month two, when she had begun to understand that it was less a guest at the door than a slow change in the weather inside the room. The room had been getting colder for a long time. The room would, eventually, be cold enough that Alice would not need to be in it. That was the whole of it. There was no doorbell.
She had been waiting, without quite admitting it, for some kind of arrival.
She thought, Well. There you are.
Alice looked at the rose. The rose looked back.
The rose was new. The rose had not been there at midnight. The rose had not been brought by any of the night staff Alice had heard come in and out, and Alice, who had been awake, would have heard.
On the windowsill, in a small clear glass that had once held a votive: a single white rose.

The room was lit only by the small under-cabinet light above the sink, the one Alice had asked the day staff to leave on at night, because the overhead was too bright and the dark was too dark and the under-cabinet was, like Alice, exactly enough. The walls were the color all hospital walls were — a beige with a slight green undertone that the manufacturer probably called sage and that Alice had been calling, privately, the color of agreed-upon endings. On the wall above the bed: a print of a beach Alice did not recognize. On the bedside table: a paper cup of water with a bent straw, the small plastic dispenser of mouth swabs the night nurse had refilled at midnight, a worn copy of the Book of Common Prayer Alice's daughter had brought on Sunday and that Alice had not, in the four days since, opened. On the floor by the door: a pair of slippers Alice had not worn in three weeks.
She would, she had decided, save her remaining laughter for herself.

She had been awake since three. She had been, in some technical sense, awake since around two-thirty, but she had spent the first half-hour pretending to be asleep so the night nurse would not come in and check on her. Alice had gotten very good, over the past five months, at pretending to be asleep. The skill had not been on her list of things she wanted to learn before she died. It was on the list now, and would, by some accounting, be one of the last skills she added. She found this funny. She had not, lately, mentioned that she found it funny, because the people around her had begun to react to her finding things funny in a way that suggested they were keeping a tally somewhere of her remaining sense of humor, and that the tally was meant to be reassuring to them rather than to her.
Alice Newsom, in Room 217, was awake.

This was not unusual. The hospice was generally quiet. The hospice was, on its quietest days, the quietest part of the building, quieter even than the chapel on the ground floor where Father Anselm offered the noon mass that almost nobody attended, quieter than the staff chapel on the third floor where the night nurses sometimes sat to cry without being seen. Hospice quiet was a particular quiet. It was the quiet of rooms in which time had begun to soften at the edges, the quiet of voices kept low not out of respect but out of sympathy with the rooms themselves, the quiet that absorbed footsteps and conversations and the small distant sounds of the city outside and gave back, in their place, the steady reliable hush of equipment doing what equipment did.
The hospice on the second floor of St. Jude's Mercy was, on the last Tuesday in April, very quiet.

Nicola Greer stood on the small landing, pale and exhausted, a duffel bag at her feet, her left hand pressed flat against her stomach in the gesture of a woman who had been making the gesture for some weeks without quite recognizing what the gesture was telling her.
Three forty-two AM. The bell rang.
The fridge cycled. The fridge cycled again.
The streetlight outside flickered, twice, in a pattern that was probably nothing.

She thought, something has been starting for some time, and tonight, in this apartment, I am going to be the one it asks to listen.
She thought, something is starting.
Sacrifice. Letting go. New perspectives.

She held it in her palm.
She picked up the Hanged Man from the windowsill.

She did not, yet, lay the cards out. The cards were not for her. The cards were going to be for Nicola, when Nicola arrived. But the cards needed to know they were going to be used. Cards, like dancers, performed better when warmed up.

Then she turned, and crossed back to the cards on the floor, and crouched, and placed the deck on the small low table she used for readings — the table that was, in the daytime, a footstool, and that was, in the nighttime when occasion required, a sacred surface.

He was middle-aged. He wore a suit that was nicer than the suits the oil-exec types wore — not flashy, just correct, in a way that suggested he had not had to think about whether it was correct. The suit was charcoal. The tie was muted. The shoes, glimpsed when he had crossed his legs, were lawyer-shoes.

He was alone. He had not ordered. He had been seated forty minutes ago and he was watching her — not the way the oil-exec types watched, not the way the regulars watched, not even the way certain of the female patrons watched (which was a category unto itself) — but the way a man watches a structural detail he has noticed and does not yet understand the significance of.
Across the dining room, at Table 14, a man Nicola did not recognize was watching her.
The world held its breath.
That’s okay. Stick around. You’ll learn.
I do not understand the metaphor of the microphone.
The life growing within her gave another insistent nudge. A countdown. A promise. An ultimatum.

Maybe the point wasn’t awareness or ignorance. Maybe it wasn’t even survival. Maybe it was just about grabbing the mic, even if your voice was cracked and broken, and screaming your goddamn song into the void until something, finally, definitively, broke.
The Empress, holding the seeds of life and oblivion in her trembling hands.
She felt Aria — the anomaly, the seeker — settling into a corner of her own consciousness like an unhoused intelligence finally locating an unlocked door.
