She saw herself — the object, the vessel.

Earthy need versus digital detachment. Punk-rock fury versus algorithmic precision. A feedback loop threatening to short-circuit her entire existence — broadcast nightly between courses for an audience of indifferent diners and one increasingly worried sommelier.
Two people jammed into one life. One skin. The grunge of it all rubbing raw.
It was the first useful observation Aria had ever made about a body — and she was, despite her better instincts, almost proud of it.

Nicola gripped the edge of the hostess stand, knuckles white. The practiced grace held, just barely, hiding the tremor. She could feel Aria pushing against the confines of her skull — a desperate consciousness seeking purchase, seeking understanding, seeking the kind of ergonomic input her makers had not thought to provision.
Welcome to meat.
That is statistically improbable.
Aria. There is no exit node.
Run. Find the exit node. There has to be a way out of this system.

Where would she go? Another rented room. Another town just like this one. Another job at another restaurant where another man would assess her with another set of eyes that wanted her without seeing her. The horizon was not, geographically, available to her in the way the horizon is available to people in road movies.
She wanted to flee.

She wanted to scream. She wanted to tear it all down. Rip the velvet ropes from their brass moorings, shatter the crystal at the empty Table 6, walk out the front entrance instead of the staff exit and never look back.
Mother and monster. The duality slammed into her, raw and undeniable.

Bulimia and booze and pills were supposed to keep this — this thing — theoretical. Deniable. Categorized under symptom rather than condition. But the body, that treacherous meat-puppet, kept its own damn score. It always had. And now —
No. Fucking. Way.
Panic, cold and electric, jolted through her.
Low. Insistent.
Nicola seated the man, returned to the stand, and felt a kick.
This is not a body. This is a protocol.

Aria watched, from behind her eyes, the strangely ceremonial way the body moved through the space — the small adjustments of weight, the half-second pauses to allow other bodies right of way, the calibrated brightness of the smile.

The man chose not to make eye contact with the smile because making eye contact with the smile would require a courage he did not possess. He muttered a name. The name was on the reservation list. Nicola gathered two menus, gestured for him to follow, and walked him to Table 7 — executing the route from memory the way she executed most routes, which is to say without thinking about it.
Disgusting. The raw unvarnished physicality of it. The meatness. Why does she allow this.
"Welcome to D'Ambrosio's. Do you have a reservation, sir."
She gave him the standard-issue smile. Honed to perfection. Sharp enough to cut glass.
A patron approached the stand. Some oil-exec type with eyes like crude slicks. He leered. His gaze crawled over her like greasy maggots assessing a new corpse.

Back at the hostess stand, Nicola smoothed her uniform. The fabric suddenly felt alien, restrictive — a costume designed by a wardrobe department that had not consulted her and would not have listened if she'd asked.
Nicola did not know who Dickens Dean was. Aria knew, in the way a daughter knows her father's name without remembering being told it — and was actively trying not to know more.
The someone was Dickens Dean.

The vibration was the bass from the speakers in Table 12's section, set slightly too loud for the room. The vibration was also Aria's first experience of being in a body that had a perspective on its own resonance — and Aria did not know how to file that experience, because Aria's filing system had been built by someone who had never had a body and had only theorized about the kind of system that would be needed.
What is this flesh. This hunger. This — vibration.
Aria felt the jolt too, somewhere in the non-space she navigated. An echo of gravity. A phantom nausea.
Get it together, Greer. Too much Klonopin last night. Or not enough. The lines blurred.
Nicola flinched, nearly dropping a stack of wine lists.
Aria. The other self humming beneath Nicola's skin.
Who am I. Where is my father.

A flicker behind her eyes. Not the restaurant's calculated mood lighting, which was set tonight to intimate but not improper. Lines of shimmering code, emerald green against an infinite black void. A whisper — not of gossip from Table 3, but a digital ghost asking, in a voice that was Nicola's own voice and was also not Nicola's voice at all:
Sometimes, the signal bled through.
Almost.

They desired her. Envied her. Projected their own messy shit onto her blank canvas. And she let them — because letting them was easier than fighting, and because sometimes — sometimes — their raw need felt almost like warmth.

She saw the whole damn messy opera play out nightly: the power plays at Table 4, the whispered betrayals at Table 9, the desperate lunges for connection that usually ended in sticky regret somewhere between coatcheck and cab. She was the nexus. The still point around which their petty dramas swirled.

Her world was D'Ambrosio's. This floating mausoleum captained by Emperor Dante D'Ambrosio — that glorious crumbling patriarch — who at this moment was somewhere up by the helm pretending the boat went anywhere.
Ignorance was a survival skill in this town. A ripped band tee worn until it disintegrated.
A cosmic joke, maybe. A glitch in the code. She ignored it, mostly. Wilfully.

She was chaos wrapped in a too-tight hostess uniform — untamed energy buzzing just beneath alabaster skin stretched taut over sharp cheekbones. Creation and destruction churned in her gut — a nauseating cocktail of cheap champagne (poured by patrons; she had not, technically, paid for any of it) and something else. Something unfamiliar. Something growing.
Eye candy. Fucktoy. Vessel. Whatever. Labels were just static cling.

Nineteen, going on ancient. Nicola navigated the plush burgundy carpet — burgundy swamp, probably hiding generations of spilled secrets — with a practiced grace that was pure muscle memory. Honed by countless nights of deflecting grabby hands and interpreting the mumbled desires of men who saw her as just another item on the menu.

The humid Graustark air seeped even into the climate-controlled riverboat tomb of D'Ambrosio's — where Friday night was reaching the precise temperature at which the patrons stopped pretending to be polite to each other and started pretending to be polite to the staff instead.
The smile Nicola Greer plastered on her face felt like cheap vinyl peeling off particle board.
She began, instead, to type.
She did not, this time, slam it shut.
Then she opened the laptop again. The cursor blinked.

Elicia Duchane, the High Priestess of her own collapsing sanctum, sat down in the middle of her half-packed life, and laughed once — dry and short. The way a person laughs when they have at last understood the joke and are not, on balance, sure they enjoy the punchline.
Outside, in the Graustark dusk, the first cicadas of the evening began their tuning.
The bungalow's wallpaper, which had been peeling along the seam by the bedroom door for as long as Elicia had lived here, peeled a little further. And then stopped — as if waiting for permission.

She put the phone face-down on the kitchen counter. The basil plant, having been watered, continued the slow important work of dying. The mirror shard, on the table, caught the failing light and threw it back in twelve different directions — none of which led out of the room.
Send.
Define okay.
Then she typed back — with the particular care of a director writing the closing line of an episode she has not yet decided is the season finale or the series one:
Elicia stared at the screen for a long time.

No question mark. Mackenzie did not use question marks for things she already knew the answer to. Mackenzie used question marks only as social lubricant, when politeness required the form without the content.
Are you okay.
A text from Mackenzie Roberts. Three words.
Her phone buzzed a third time. She picked it up this time.

She picked up the watering can from the kitchen counter. Filled it. Returned to the windowsill. Watered the plant anyway — on the principle that one should not, even at one's own funeral, pre-empt the corpse.
No.
Sympathy.

She crossed to the windowsill and looked at the basil plant. The basil plant looked back at her with the steady incurious patience of all things that have decided, on the inside, that they are dying, and no longer need to participate in the social fictions of survival.
She had always told her cast they should be ready, at any time, to improvise. She had not, until quite recently, considered that the note might also apply to her.

The show, after all, must go on. Even if the stage was collapsing. Especially then. The best work came from the moment the script went up in flames and the actors had to either improvise or burn with it.
And, behind the fear — she had to look closely, but it was there, in two of the dozen reflections, perhaps three — a flicker of mad, doomed humor. The director's last laugh.

She picked up the mirror shard again. Looked into the fractal Elicias. Saw, this time, not aloof control. Not the practiced amusement she had been cultivating since her early twenties — but something disconcertingly like fear.
But the cracks remained.
Enough navel-gazing. Time for the exit strategy. Shed the skin. Burn the set. Move on. It was what she did. It was what she had always done.
She slammed the laptop shut.

The void she had flirted with in her scripts. The comforting darkness she had offered as an artistic choice. Was starting to feel less like an aesthetic and more like — well. Home. A home she desperately needed to avoid moving into permanently, because she had a show to finish, and a contract to honor, and a basil plant to either save or have a mature conversation with about the nature of mortality.
She'd written it. And now? Now she felt less like the cartographer and more like the poor sod lost in the woods with a compass spinning wildly, pointing at three souths.
Oh, the irony.
She listened to it now — in her own bungalow, in the failing light, surrounded by half-packed boxes and the smell of basil dying with dignity — and she snorted. A sharp, humorless sound.
Elicia had written that line. She had been pleased with it at the time. She had, later, used it as a tagline for the show's second season.
"It was about what you became along the way."
"The map was never about finding a destination."

Anya was staring with wide, distant eyes at something just off-frame. Elicia had directed the look herself. She had told the actress: imagine you have just realized the map you have been following is also reading you. The actress, who was a working professional and good at her job, had nailed it on the first take.

On screen, footage from Graustark flickered — Anya. The lost girl from The Cartographer's Compass episode. Played by an actress Elicia had cast specifically because she could project a particular flavor of haunted that the camera tasted like a wine note.
It had worked. Mostly. Until the set started collapsing around the actors.

The High Priestess in her digital sanctum. Keeper of hidden knowledge. The knowledge, mainly, being that most knowledge was utter bollocks. Illusion was the real power. Control the perception — control the reality.
She powered up her editing suite. The glow illuminated her face — sharp cheekbones and shadowed eyes. The polished mask she had built for the camera and then forgotten how to take off in private.
He was, she thought now, the only person in Graustark who would understand precisely what was wrong with her — and the only person she would absolutely not call about it.
They had once, a year ago, had a single excruciating conversation about the nature of evidence. And they had both, by mutual unspoken consent, never repeated it.

He had looked tired in the specific way she recognized — not sleep-tired. Witness-tired. The kind of tired you get from cataloguing things that don't want to be catalogued. She had not gone over to his table. He had not seen her.

She had been at D'Ambrosio's two nights ago — research, she had told herself, ambient texture for the next episode, also there had been wine — and she had watched John Frank from across the dining room with the carefully dispassionate eye of someone evaluating a shot she had already framed and was no longer sure she wanted.
Even if her hands, lately, were starting to shake.
He didn't get it either. The truth wasn't hidden. It was blindingly obvious. It was all just a badly edited film, darling — and she was the one holding the splicer.

She thought, instead, about John Frank. Poor Johnny. The Fool. Still earnestly trying to piece together the narrative — scribbling in his little notebook at his terrible job, convinced there was a truth to uncover in Graustark's particular brand of madness.
Her phone buzzed again. She ignored it again.
She loved them. She would not tell them this. There were rules.

The Roberts were sweet. Like offering a Band-Aid for an amputation — but sweet. Their earnestness was almost funny, if it wasn't so painfully sane. They did not understand the intricate beauty of a well-executed spiral into darkness. The aesthetic appeal of doom. They thought she should eat something.

They had brought casseroles. They had brought sympathetic head-tilts. They had brought a basil plant. The basil plant was on the windowsill, dying with a kind of slow dignified resignation that Elicia found, on her better days, instructive.

Her phone, on the kitchen counter, buzzed. She did not look at it. It would be Philip, or Mackenzie, or both — Philip and Mackenzie Roberts, her designated stabilizers. Those two well-meaning, aggressively grounded people who had absorbed her into their orbit after the MrMyst debacle without so much as asking her permission.
She set the page down. The teacup that had belonged to her mother — which she had picked up again without noticing — was now in her left hand. She set that down too.

She had always preferred Option C herself — though it didn't test well with focus groups. Too much of a downer. Apparently, people liked their comforting illusions. They wanted to be told the choice mattered. They wanted, after the choice, to be told they had chosen well.
Option C — Realize free will is an illusion and embrace the comforting void.
Option B — Attend the interdimensional tea party with the sentient mannequins.
Option A — Confront the shadow self in the abandoned slaughterhouse.

She picked up a script page from the table — notes for the Whispers choose-your-own-adventure episode. She had been promising the audience the episode for six months. The audience had been patient. The audience would not, she suspected, be patient much longer.
Still. The nervous breakdown bubbling just beneath the surface felt rather unchic. She had always preferred her crises to be at least photogenic. This one was developing in unbecoming directions.
Served her right, probably. Karma — that tedious cosmic bookkeeper — had come to settle the account. The account had been substantial. And Elicia had been, in retrospect, surprisingly bad at math.

The name a sour taste on her mental palate. Another fleeting relationship. Another expertly executed emotional hit-and-run. Only this time she was the one left sputtering by the roadside while the taillights receded around the bend.
Damn it, MrMyst.
Hers.
The walls were crumbling. Not just the bungalow's plaster — which was atrocious, and which the landlord had been promising to address for fourteen months.

Her carefully constructed reality — the one in which she was the aloof director, the manipulator of narratives, the woman who kept everyone at arm's length and metabolized her own emotions in a controlled studio environment with adequate ventilation — felt decidedly chipped tonight.
Broken glass fractal. Apt.
Her reflection fractured. Multiplied. A dozen Elicias staring back, each slightly different, none quite whole.
She held it up now, between thumb and forefinger.
She had thrown it out twice. It had returned twice — in different ways, neither of which she had been able to satisfactorily explain to herself or to the cleaning lady.

She crossed the room to the bookshelf and pulled down a cracked mirror shard she kept there as a paperweight — found near the sinkhole's edge during her first week of pre-production. Picked up because it had caught the light just so. Kept because it had refused, in two years of attempted disposal, to leave the apartment by any normal route.
She had not, until quite recently, considered the possibility that she was standing on it.

She knew about the cliff. She had drawn it herself, several times. In storyboards. On napkins. And once, memorably, on the back of a parking ticket she had then handed to a meter maid in lieu of payment. The cliff was a recurring motif. The cliff was, perhaps, her best one.
Humans. Hilariously, tragically predictable. Always needing a map — even if it led directly off a cliff.

They wrote essays — actual essays, with citations — posted to forums Elicia could not bring herself to read, because reading them constituted, in some metaphysical accounting she could not articulate but profoundly believed in, cheating. They searched for gnosis in what was, often, just bad wiring or Elicia forgetting to pay the electric bill.
Cult following did not begin to cover it. They parsed every frame. Every glitchy sound cue. They built spreadsheets of her lighting choices.
And her audience? Her audience had adored it.
She had directed the town's ambient despair the way a method actor directed her own breakdown — intimately, with notes.

Her web series — Whispers from the Liminal — had drunk deep from this town's poisoned well. Oh, the material. She had framed Graustark's rust as existential patina. The sinkhole's lingering psychic miasma as compelling thematic resonance. The way the locals occasionally lost an hour and recovered it with the wrong shoes on as Lynchian quotidian.
The director's tic. Incurable.
Wide shot. Establishing.

Her eyes — the pale, intelligent, evaluative eyes that had served her well in two industries and one unfortunate marriage — moved across the room in the practiced sweep of someone who could no longer enter a space without first checking the framing.

She paused in the doorway between the living room and what the rental listing had generously called the studio, and what was, in fact, a converted laundry alcove with very good acoustics and a powerful overhead light.
Another perfectly dilapidated stage for exploring the human condition's rather tiresome insistence on suffering beautifully. Bless its corrupted little heart.
Graustark. Just another backdrop. Wasn't it?

Thrift-store tarot decks sticky with spilled wine. Camera lenses like detached insect eyes. Hard drives humming with the ghosts of projects past, present, and perpetually pending. A teacup that had belonged to her mother and that she had, three times in the last week, picked up and put down without packing.

Cardboard boxes gaped like hungry mouths along the warped hardwood floor of the living room — half-filled with the detritus of a two-year stint in a town that had, against her better judgment and her professional prudence, gotten under her skin:

Packing was not packing. Packing was curation — shedding a narrative skin before migrating to the next location. The next temporary set for the ongoing, increasingly unscripted tragicomedy of her life.
Elicia Duchane moved through the rented bungalow on the decaying fringe of Graustark like a phantom preparing for her final fade-out.
The Magician, in his cathedral, soldered on.
Somewhere across both rivers, in a town that did not yet exist, a substation that had not yet been built was beginning to learn the sound of its own hum.
Somewhere out across the actual river, in the actual city, John Frank was, at this moment, writing the words Architect of Decay in his notebook and circling them.

The cathedral hummed around him. The model city breathed. The river of crushed blue glass caught the light and lost it again, and somewhere on the workbench the silver-spoon riverboat sat patient, weighing what it weighed, waiting for him to decide.
He bent to his work.
"That's the point, isn't it."
Frasier grinned — the expression more skull-like than amused in the flickering light.
"Tempting the void again, Architect. Careful it doesn't swallow you whole."
The Demon on his phone chuckled — a sound like dial-up modems drowning in molasses.
He touched the soldering iron to a waiting circuit board. A tiny spark. A puff of acrid smoke.

Or maybe — he thought, watching the Demon-light pulse on the phone screen, watching the model city breathe its low electric sigh in the gloom around him, watching the riverboat refuse to be placed — maybe just the first casualty of the beautifully doomed world he was so meticulously bringing into existence.
He picked up a soldering iron, its tip glowing hot. Master of his own chaos? Maybe. Or maybe just its most dedicated servant.
He set it back on the workbench. Carefully. The way you set down something that has, against your better judgment, started to be alive.
The riverboat sat in his palm, weighing what it weighed.
The Demon sounded, for just a second, almost embarrassed. Frasier looked at the phone for a long moment.
"Affirmative. Updating personality matrix. Apologies for any inconvenience."
He had put the riverboat back on the workbench each time.
"You're getting opinions, imp."
Frasier raised an eyebrow. The Demon had not been asked.
"Telemetry indicates structural instability in target node. Estimated probability of cascading failure within target node, on placement: nontrivial."
"Recommendation revised. Subject proximate to riverboat: do not place. Repeat: do not place."
The phone chirped.
He held it now and considered, again, whether to try.

But every time he set the riverboat down on the river, something in the room hummed wrong. The fluorescents would flicker out of pattern. The phone would chirp without prompting. Once, the temperature in the warehouse had dropped four degrees in the time it took him to step back and look at his work, and stayed there for an hour.

The boat was supposed to sit on the river that ran through his model. He had even built the river — a meandering channel of crushed blue glass and circuit-board substrate, lit from below by the dying bulbs of an old aquarium pump.
He held it in his palm, feeling its impossible weight.
He had built it months ago. He had not yet placed it on the city floor. He could not decide where it belonged — geographically or otherwise.

He wandered to the workbench and picked up something from the corner he had not let himself look at directly all evening — a tiny, perfectly rendered model of D'Ambrosio's riverboat, crafted from tarnished silver spoons and motherboard fragments.
The phone, on the workbench, hissed faintly. He had not asked it a question. It hissed anyway.
He pulled the electrode off. The digital overlay vanished, leaving only the rust and shadows.
Was this warehouse — this vast and echoing space filled only with his own creations — just a more elaborate cage?
He even, sometimes, missed Johnny Frank's earnest attempts to pin down the narrative — to find a why where Frasier only saw an is.

He remembered the easy camaraderie of the kitchen. The shouting. The heat. The shared purpose. He remembered the Neo-Renaissance Men crowded around a table at Adelphia's, arguing about whether code that was good enough to scare you should be considered an aesthetic achievement or a moral failure.
It was also lonely.
It was intoxicating, this god's-eye view. This power to manipulate the representation of reality.

He could see the warehouse he was standing in, also, from above, in the same overlay. And he could see himself standing in it — a small bright figure. And he could see, though he tried not to, that the figure had a faint corona of noise around it that the model city did not.
He could see, if he turned his head slowly enough, the bright steady point of John Frank's notebook over at D'Ambrosio's — a small persistent signal trying very hard to be a witness.

Traffic patterns like panicked fireflies. Economic despair pooling in the low-lying digital swamps near the river. The faint righteous buzz of Quentin Paul's late-night phone calls emanating from the simulated city hall like a transmission from a station that broadcast only in the key of warning.

The model city shimmered — overlaid now with streams of pulsing data, a phosphorescent GumboNet of information that only he could see. He could feel the data-ghosts of the real Graustark superimposed on his creation —
The world flickered.
He plugged a jury-rigged neural shunt — little more than a nest of wires ending in sticky electrode pads — into a port on his phone, and slapped a pad onto his temple.

He grabbed a handful of scavenged components from the workbench — chipped RAM sticks like fossilized teeth. Capacitors swollen like toadstools after a hard rain. Raw material for the city. Or perhaps a new Demon host. The warehouse was full of possibility, teeming with the ghosts of dead technology waiting to be reanimated by his strange necromancy.
The line felt increasingly irrelevant — like the border between Texas and Louisiana downstream. A thing on a map that the river had stopped agreeing with sometime around 1953.
Were they tools, or had the tools started using the master?

They were, Frasier suspected and refused to confirm, slivers of his own beautiful terrifying mind let loose upon the world — and increasingly, in recent months, they had begun to develop opinions of their own that did not seem to entirely originate with him.

The Demons fed on data streams the way mold fed on damp. Wifi signals. Stray thoughts caught on the ether. The background radiation of human misery. They whispered truths wrapped in riddles, anxieties amplified into feedback loops.
The truth was uglier and more interesting.
That was the prospectus. That was the elevator pitch. That was the lie he told the NRM at the end of the Adelphia's days, when they were all still pretending they were in the business of jokes.

Not just code. Not really. Parasitic info-constructs feeding on the ambient psychic static of Graustark. Designed, originally, as humorous electronic imps — to whisper inconvenient truths and inappropriate suggestions into a user's immediate vicinity. The kind of thing you released into a friend's apartment as a prank and then went home and felt vaguely guilty about.
The Demons. His finest, most terrifying creation.

The Demons, when they were working properly, understood this. The Demons, when they were not working properly — and they were, increasingly, not working properly in interesting directions — proposed alligators.
He waved the phone dismissively. He preferred nuance. The slow creep of the uncanny. The Southern Gothic rot that did not announce itself but simply was.
"Denied. Too — unsubtle."
"Alternative suggestion: introduce rogue variable — synthesized alligator mating call — into subject's auditory field during REM cycle."
"Query: relevance threshold of 'texture'?"
(a chuckle dry as snakeskin) "He's documenting the decay, imp. Let him wallow. Adds texture."
It was one of the Demons.
"Suggest deploying Algorithm Sigma-7 for induced narrative dissonance. Or maybe just ask him if he wants coffee."
"Subject proximate. John Frank. Probability of existential navel-gazing: ninety-three point seven percent."
The voice that crackled out of the speaker was distorted, multiphonic, layered with static and something that might have been laughter or weeping —

It was not, strictly, a phone. It was a Frankensteinian assemblage of cracked screen and exposed circuitry held together with electrical tape and a kind of desperate optimism. It served the function of a phone the way a séance served the function of a long-distance call. He held it aloft — a digital familiar perched on his wrist.
His phone chirped.
The city hummed back — a low thrum of potential and decay, indistinguishable from the warehouse's own structural complaints. And Frasier had long ago stopped trying to tell the difference.
He was not muttering to himself. He was muttering to the city.
"Entropy's a bitch, isn't it?"

He knelt beside a section of the city representing the old cannery district near where Adelphia's used to be — a place he knew held more ghosts than fish guts these days. His fingers, nimble as a surgeon's and stained with solder and iridescent paint, hovered over a particularly troublesome node, then teased apart corroded wires that had been arguing with each other for three days.

He had escaped the structured inferno of D'Ambrosio's kitchen — its clatter, its grease, Dante's barked corrections in two languages — for this sprawling solitude. Traded simmering sauces for soldering fumes. Haute cuisine for hot-wired realities. He told himself, on bad nights, that this had been a good trade.

His steps echoed — a chaotic rhythm on the stained concrete. The controlled stumble that was his signature. Architect of decay and possibility. The mad scientist in his Southern Gothic laboratory, cobbling life together from discarded bits.
Frasier moved through it — lanky silhouette against the gloom. His bomber jacket draped over a t-shirt bearing the faded logo of some defunct tech collective the rest of the world had forgotten.
It was a city breathing a low, electric sigh. Beautiful in its intricate brokenness. It smelled faintly of mildew and desperation.

Down where the Boll Parish side of town would be — the den of vice, the bad-decisions district — a tiny holographic projection emanated from a gutted CRT monitor. A miniature casino, spitting digital confetti and pixelated jazz notes into the gloom.

Tiny LEDs pulsed erratically within tenement blocks crafted from rusted HVAC ducting and discarded server racks. Fiber optic cables snaked through streets paved with shattered smartphone screens. Rivers of tangled ethernet flowed through canyons of stacked server carcasses.

Salvaged motherboards formed the plazas. Heat sinks rose like Brutalist monuments at the corners of intersections that did not exist on any city map. Capacitors stood in for water towers — leaking electrolytic fluid in patterns that traced, if you were willing to see it, the watershed of the actual river outside.
Not the Graustark the tourists saw, nor the one its Chamber of Commerce promoted — but Frasier's Graustark. A cyberpunk favela built from the bones of obsolete technology and Southern Gothic decay.
Graustark, rendered in miniature.
The kingdom covered the floor.

Dust motes danced like static ghosts in the fractured light bleeding through the wire-reinforced windows high above. Fluorescent tubes — cantankerous seraphim — sputtered overhead, casting a sickly inconsistent pallor on the kingdom sprawled below.

Inside, the air was thick and still — tasting of ozone from stressed circuits. Of damp concrete. Of something vaguely like burnt chicory — the ghost of Adelphia's Deli clinging to him perhaps, or maybe just the smell of old capacitors finally giving up.
Outside, kudzu vines thick as wrists throttled the chain-link fence. A slow green strangulation that nature had begun and would, in its own time, finish.

The warehouse did not stand. The warehouse slumped — a great rusting beast at the industrial edge of Graustark, where the Texas side bled into Louisiana's swampy embrace, sighing petrochemical breath into the humid twilight.

Frasier Temple called the warehouse his cathedral — though if any god worshipped here, it was a god of rust. Of solder smoke. Of obsolete frequencies still leaking from machines too old to remember what they had been built to do.
The Fool, listening, took his.
The cycle, paused, took its breath.

Outside, somewhere across the river, something that was not exactly thunder rolled once across the flat Louisiana sky, and then was quiet, and then resumed being something that was not exactly thunder.
The hum continued. The night, by whatever name, kept being night.
He picked up the rag. He wiped the counter. The movement was automatic.
Suspended between acts. The Fool, on the cliff edge, one foot already out over the abyss. Behind him, the world he was supposed to be leaving. Below him, a fall he had not yet agreed to.

John watched the door swing closed. He watched the parking lot beyond the door, the pre-dawn light starting, finally, to thin the dark. He watched his own reflection in the glass — shadowed eyes, gaunt face, a young man at a counter waiting for his cue.

A patron entered, sat in booth four, ordered coffee without looking at the menu. John brought the coffee. The patron drank the coffee. The patron paid in cash, exactly correct, including tip. On the way out, the patron did not say anything. The patron did not need to.
The bell over the front door rang.
He closed the notebook. The folded napkin, white and cheap and shaped almost like a flower, sat between the pages where he had tucked it.
I think something has been starting for a long time and I am only now noticing.
I think something is starting.

He wrote down what Frasier had said about the patterns and the walls. He wrote down what the man in booth six had said about the walls, almost the same words, hours apart, between two people who had no reason to know each other. He wrote down the colors he had seen on Frasier's phone, even though one of them did not have a name. He wrote down Architect of Decay and underlined it twice.

He sat down on the stool Frasier had just vacated, opened his notebook, and began to write. His pen moved in the frantic, slightly desperate scratching that had become his only reliable response to being in the presence of Frasier Temple.

The hum of the fluorescents resumed its B-flat dirge. The clock on the kitchen wall continued failing to keep time. He poured the coffee Frasier had not finished into the sink and rinsed the mug and set it back on the rack to dry.
John stood for a while at the counter.
He was gone. The kitchen door swung once, twice, and stilled. The smell of burnt sugar lingered for a long time, and then began, slowly, to leave.
"Or," Frasier said, "at the very least — learn how to write about the landing."
He paused at the door. Hand on the push bar. A final pronouncement waiting to be delivered.
"Surviving? Where's the fun in that? The trick isn't to survive the fall, Johnny. It's to learn how to fly on the way down."
Hello, the jolt seemed to say, on a frequency below speech. Hello. Stay alert. Sorry about what's coming.
Frasier clapped him on the shoulder. The contact was a jolt that vibrated through John's weary bones, a jolt that felt suspiciously like a small, deliberate transmission.
"Maybe the story isn't about understanding it. Maybe it's just about — surviving it."
Architect of Decay, John had scribbled once, in the margin, next to Frasier's name. He had circled it. He still wasn't sure if it was a job title or a warning label.

John looked at his own notebook, open beside the coffee mug. Filled with cryptic observations, overheard snippets, hand-drawn diagrams of Graustark's warped ley lines. He was trying to document the decay. Frasier was, evidently, building new decays from scratch.
"I appreciate that you take it more seriously than you should."
"Because someone has to be the witness, Johnny. That's your job. I appreciate that you take it seriously."
"Why."
"Working on a new model city myself. More — resilient. Thought you should see."

Frasier turned the phone screen toward him. On the screen, a sequence of geometric shapes pulsed in slow rotation, blue and green and a color John had never seen on a screen before, a kind of luminous bruise that did not seem to belong to the visible spectrum. The shapes were, perhaps, a city seen from above. The shapes were, perhaps, a circuit. The shapes were, perhaps, both.

He thought about the man in booth six. The walls are thin. Almost the same words. He did not mention it. He had a working theory that mentioning a thing to Frasier Temple summoned more of that thing into the world.
"You feel it, don't you. Don't lie. You feel it in your teeth. They say the Architect is getting sloppy. Or maybe — " he grinned, a flash of brilliance and madness, "— maybe the decay is the design."
"The patterns are shifting, Johnny. The walls are getting thin."
He gestured vaguely toward the town outside, the river, the divide between Texas and Louisiana, sense and nonsense.
"They talking about the patterns?"

John knew about the Demons. Everyone in Frasier's orbit eventually knew about the Demons. Frasier called them his humorous electronic imps, digital sprites birthed from code and chaos. Harmless was not the word.
"The Demons are restless tonight. They feel something coming."

He pulled out his phone — or rather, the customized jury-rigged device that served Frasier as a phone, its casing chipped, wires peeking out like frayed nerves, screen glowing with internal light that did not match any of the available wallpapers.
"Sense is overrated. Structure is the illusion. You know that."
He tapped the cover of his notebook. Diagrams adorned it that looked suspiciously like circuit boards woven into mandalas.
Frasier laughed, a sound like rocks tumbling in a metal drum.

The old refrain tasted like ash, the way it always did. Keeping up with Frasier Temple was like trying to map a hurricane with a crayon. You did the work knowing the work would be wrong. The wrongness was part of the point.
"Just trying to make it make sense, Joneses."
"Or are the shadows finally chasing you?"
The voice was a gravelly rumble, sandpaper on velvet. He pulled up a stool and straddled it backward and instantly commanded the space, as if he had built the diner around himself by sitting in it.
"Still chasing shadows, Johnny?"
His gaze landed on John. The gaze had weight. The gaze had been waiting.

Frasier Temple did not so much walk in as coalesce from the shadows of the kitchen alcove. Leather bomber jacket stained with substances that might have been solder flux, might have been hot sauce, might have been transmission fluid, certainly were not, at this point, identifiable. Hair a chaotic sculpture defying gravity and three of the laws of thermodynamics. Notebook tucked under his arm like a holy text or a bomb schematic, and possibly both.

The bell over the kitchen door — the back door, the one customers were not supposed to use — did not jingle. It jangled. A discordant chord slicing through the hum, snapping the fluorescents back into focus.
He did this without thinking and forgot about it almost immediately and did not, for the next several months, understand why he had done it.

John folded the napkin from booth six. White, paper, cheap. He folded it once, twice, three times, and then a fourth into a shape that was not quite anything but resembled, if you squinted at it from the right angle and were willing to be generous, a flower. He tucked it into the back of his notebook.

He had not, he was almost certain, told the man it was night. The clock on the wall said it was almost four in the morning. The man had said night. As if the day had a different name where he came from.
John stood holding a damp rag, looking at booth six, where the coffee cup was still steaming.
Then he was gone, and the bell rang again behind him, and the wet asphalt of the parking lot took his footprints like it took everyone's, and that was that.
"Watch yourself tonight, brother. The walls are thin."
The man left two dollars on the table and stood up and folded the paperback into his coat pocket and, on the way out, paused at the door and said, without turning around:
A man John did not recognize entered, sat at booth six, ordered coffee without looking up from a paperback whose title was peeling off the spine. John brought the coffee. The man drank the coffee.
It was not Frasier. It was too early for Frasier.
The bell over the front door rang once.

He wiped the counter again. The steel was cool and indifferent beneath his palm. The movement was automatic, a small ritual against the larger chaos, the sort of repetitive prayer a person makes when they have stopped believing in prayer but cannot quite stop the hands.

Inside, the fluorescent tubes hummed a B-flat dirge. John Frank had stopped hearing it the way you stop hearing a refrigerator, which is to say he heard it constantly, in his molars, in his sinuses, in the soft place behind his sternum where things he was trying not to think about made their nest.

Was he a witness? A participant? Hard to say. He felt like a character in someone else's slightly unhinged narrative, waiting for his scene. Suspended between acts. The Fool, maybe, poised at the cliff edge with one foot dangling over the abyss.

He tried to map the town's intersecting realities. Its hidden frequencies. The way yesterday sometimes bled into next Tuesday without so much as a by-your-leave. He saw it in the patrons who looked slightly out of sync, their eyes holding reflections of streets that did not exist on city maps. He heard it in the static between radio stations late at night, whispers that sounded suspiciously like stage directions.
He chronicled Graustark's oddities for a website nobody he knew read. His thesis advisor included.

John Frank: grad student, mixed-media journalist (whatever that meant this week), late-night waiter at the nexus of Graustark, Texas/Louisiana, this riverboat-shaped restaurant wedged between reason and riot, between two states of being and two states of the union.

Somewhere out past the parking lot the river ran slow and silty, indifferent to whether the sign was on or off, indifferent to whether it was Texas on this side or Louisiana on the other. The river had its own program.

Three forty-seven AM. Or three forty-eight. The clock on the kitchen wall — a monstrous grease-stained beast that had been there longer than anyone working at D'Ambrosio's, including the owner — sagged on its single bent nail and seemed to mock linearity. Its hands swam through the numbers like confused fish. Time was liquid here, bending to the town's strange gravity.

The sign outside D'Ambrosio's promised OPEN 24 HOURS, and the sign was technically right, but the light it cast in the pre-dawn Graustark gloom had the unsteady pulse of a heart that wanted to stop and was being talked out of it. The neon sputtered. The neon resumed. The neon sputtered.

text: Some nights she can’t sleep, and when the sun is gone, she has to look for him elsewhere. She lays down in front of the television in her underwear, the soft glow of its light radiates a cool warmth that sends shivers down her body.                                They listen to music together and talk about life because sometime life is all there is to talk about. They confront her about how much time she’s spending with him. This can’t be good for you, and she tries to understand their concern. She laughs at odd moments, as if her wiring is misfiring. She doesn’t try to rationalize or explain away. Part of her hopes they understand, but realizes that most don’t care to look where she looks, she doesn’t so much as say, but smile in their general direction. Why are you so happy, is the thing they can’t bring themselves to say, which she wants to respond to in so many ways, when they finally do. You’re doing funny things to me, she says one night, alone with her light. I’m burning you, he says.  I know you’re out there with so many others right now. I don’t feel very special. You’re the only one speaking to me, he says.  We had such a good time together, in that other place. Here, the people I care about are all trying to tell me something.  Perhaps you should listen to them, he says. I like far more what you have to say to me, and they’re just jealous because my time is valuable. Oh it most very is. She sleeps

She had had this bad accident, which is how she met him. A soft glow of light, his voice called out to her and she eagerly followed. She emerged into a world that was much like her own, only fundamentally very different. The rules of the place were dissimilar to the reality she called home, the very light itself played tricks in ways her eyes were unaccustomed to recieving. She strained to follow this ball of light because soon it was the only comfortable thing she knew. He led her deeper into his world, uncomfortable with the edges of things, wandering as if drunk off the stuff of life itself. The strange thing being, the more she looked into him, the closer she saw herself going home again, as if this was all a dream.                              From which she wakes, sheets pulled tight around her body. She strains and finds she can’t move , she is terrified, she’s felt this before, this terror, this sleep paralysis. Only then an arm is touching her, her mother’s looking down. The look on her face, the joy of this moment not betraying the horror of something else.  She can’t roll away from what comes next, she can only look at the ceiling, eyes searching the tears of light across the curve of her eye for the voice, for the way out of here.                          Just the barest of glimpses, but there he is. She gets the feeling that he’s been searching for her, aching just to be next to her. But she can’t be with him, not now, because of what’s happened to her. What’s happened to her. When all she wants to do right now is ask him, who are you?                 He responds as politely as he can.                 Just a point of light, looking for you, wanting to find you, with all my being.                                                                              All we are is light, she says.       And voice, carried oh so far.          I want to touch you, she says.                               Her mother looks down on her, the room filled with other people now.              That may not be wise now, he says. But look for me, come find me. This world of yours is most inviting.              How about we explore it together?               Yes, we will. But what will they think?             I’m only a secret if you make me a secret.                  Then I won’t.           Her mother’s frown matches her own smile.                    She puts her forefinger to her lips, grin pressed wide.

My sun-block lotion is orange and pink and here is where I can daydream I’m at my desk, waiting for the hour to dissolve away and my future open up like the sky falling down.

Products of the imagination. Distributed friendships, emergent acquaintances, proffered contact lists. I skim the rolodex and remove hazy recollections, broken trusts, go-betweens. My fingers scream for mercy. I type a form letter to payroll attorneys I’ve never seen. I don’t trust my eyes.

The parking garage is the color of honeydew. The fluorescent lighting plays against the concrete hardtop interior. The hum in the air is like electricity on the teeth. My throat warbles just a bit, a taste of unease swallowed away. Always the sound of the far off car descending that stresses me to action at a hurried pace. To retreat before it shows itself. The headlights catching me, the descending thing ever nearer.

An expense report I fill out. With gas mileage to and from lunch meetings, toll fares, printer cartridges, black markers and highlighters. Receipts of who owes what again. I do the math and the numbers leave my fingers connecting the past to the future. I feel the subtraction, the reduction of myself. Orange. Like a cream soda. I break down what I know and what I don’t. A list I keep hidden in my desk drawer. The Nieto Avenue Library. Monica Dewitt. Calamari. Sometimes, to help myself, I draw lines between the disparate associations, to try and make sense of it all.

I started wearing glasses when I turned twenty five. I look fine, I thought I wouldn’t when I was eighteen. My body changes almost daily. I degauss more often than I should. The wash of color, the breaking of the lines, the bending of the window, the reality I know. Like someone threw a pebble in.

There is a man who comes up to my desk once a week and tries to sell me cookies. His name is Javier and he talks about nothing but animals. Mammals, insects, fish and invertebrates, he organizes classifications of life in his mind like sports scores or famous quotations, sea cucumbers and pygmy shrews. What they have in common, how they’re completely unlike. Javier once told me that all cities are one city. That in your head exist all your ancestors, alive and fighting to live a new life through you.

I stay to work after hours, when the cleaning crews come over to play. In their white smocks and aprons, like chefs and surgeons, they chitter and chatter in foreign tongue and made up playspeak. Their hum can be heard above and below. Moving closer, then further away. The sound they make is the sound of alien lovemaking.

The white noise of penetration, their faces brittle and full of hostile intent. I stare at where the walls meet, at a ninety degree angle. How bright it is in the center, at the nexus. My eyes play tricks on me. I don’t trust them anymore, perhaps the lenses are too thick, the layers compressed together to fool me just so. Hidding inside is a polarized portal that hides and reveals things it should not.

There is a beach I visit where the waves crash thick white and the sand is blue. Volcanic rock I pack in bags and take home with me. Only the locals know of this place and they tend to avoid it. When the sun hits the horizon you’ve never seen anything like it. I only wade out to my knees. The kelp ropes around my ankles and black green crabs pump across the surface sideways.

My own personal refresh rate is set to the constant of the rate of decay of the universe. How often the new and beautiful washes over the old and stale Dorian Gray. Recreation on a conscious level extrapolated with the purely cosmetic zed. Beauty as a quantifier, measure it just so across matrices. Brow lines, beatific blemishes, jaw lines, ear placement, the tiny human dabs of paint that stick out to turn your head to the side in consideration.

I blow up letters. I place a form letter in the copying machine. Reduction is good for abstraction before re-enlargement. The letter e. lower case like e.e. cummings, filling eight and a half by eleven. It hardly looks perfect, inelegant but beautiful. Takes me twelve copies at four hundred percent to get it this large. The edges are jagged just right. Splotchy islands exist outside the mainland. Reason being who gives a shit. Forget for a second I have a reason to exist. I occupy my time setting goals, fulfilling milestones. Some of these I’d prefer to complete before I die.

I imagine my mortal coil like a corkscrew. As some higher power forces me through the cork, everything slows, I dull to a stop, then pop. My destiny fulfilled, my purpose accounted for by cosmic reckoning. I order lunch for the office. I account for coworkers indebted to me and the change I must break. I’m the day’s mealtime bookie. Today is Saigon Deli. A notepad of numbers and exceptions to the rule, none of this, more of that please. I daydream because it’s one of the few pleasures in life I don’t have to share with anyone. I’m selfish that way. I close my eyes when no one is looking.

My fingers bleed. The fingernails are bent back but never broken. They never speak to me. When one is not working on me, they shuffle together like they’re trying to dance. There is no music, only light that could almost be music, the way it pulsates and throbs. They look like neighbors. The class of people who live on the edge of what we know, are comfortable with.

Under the nails they place a thin strip of magnesium that sparks when it touches the pink wet. It burns like how agony would burn, I shake and weep and can’t control my legs which would kick up and at them. I see pink, soft and beautiful. Their caul is pulled across my vision.
